Acne.advice: Common skin condition caused by hair follicles plugging with oil and dead skin cells. Treatment is tailored to severity.
Acne.cautions: Avoid squeezing or picking, which can lead to scarring. Be patient as treatments often take 4-8 weeks to show results.
Acne.complications: Pemanent scarring (pitted or raised), post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, and psychological distress.
Acne.solutions: Topical retinoids, benzoyl peroxide, antibiotics (topical or oral), and in severe cases, isotretinoin.
Acne.doctor_advice: Consult a dermatologist for severe, painful deep cysts or if OTC treatments fail after 2 months.
Acne.symptoms: Whiteheads, blackheads, small red tender bumps (papules), pimples (pustules), and painful lumps (nodules/cysts).
Acne.prevention: Wash face twice daily with mild cleanser, choose 'non-comedogenic' products, and avoid greasy hair/skin products.
Acne.locations: Face, forehead, chest, upper back, and shoulders.
Acne.diagnosis: Primarily clinical examination; occasionally hormonal testing if suspecting underlying conditions like PCOS.
Acne.immediate_actions: Stop using harsh scrubs. Switch to a gentle cleanser and non-oily moisturizer.
Acne.lifestyle: Maintain a low-glycemic diet and manage stress levels. Wash pillowcases frequently.

Actinic Keratosis.advice: A precancerous skin growth caused by years of sun exposure. Early treatment can prevent it from turning into skin cancer.
Actinic Keratosis.cautions: Protect your skin from the sun. If left untreated, some AKs can develop into squamous cell carcinoma.
Actinic Keratosis.complications: Transformation into invasive squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) or secondary infection.
Actinic Keratosis.solutions: Cryotherapy (freezing), topical creams (fluorouracil, imiquimod), or photodynamic therapy.
Actinic Keratosis.doctor_advice: Consult a dermatologist for any rough, scaly patches that persist or bleed.
Actinic Keratosis.symptoms: Rough, dry, scaly patches of skin; often feels like sandpaper. May itch or sting.
Actinic Keratosis.prevention: Strict sun protection: SPF 30+, protective clothing, and avoiding peak sun hours.
Actinic Keratosis.locations: Sun-exposed areas: face, scalp (in bald men), ears, neck, and back of hands.
Actinic Keratosis.diagnosis: Clinical examination by a dermatologist; skin biopsy if suspicious.
Actinic Keratosis.immediate_actions: Take photos of the lesion and schedule a skin check with a dermatologist.
Actinic Keratosis.lifestyle: Wear wide-brimmed hats and use daily broad-spectrum sunscreen.

Age Spots.advice: This condition (Age Spots) should be monitored. Consult a healthcare professional for a precise diagnosis.
Age Spots.cautions: Avoid self-medicating without a professional's advice. Do not scratch or irritate the affected area.
Age Spots.complications: Secondary infections, scarring, or potential spread if not managed correctly.
Age Spots.solutions: Treatment varies by case. Typically include topical creams, proper hygiene, or specialized medical procedures.
Age Spots.doctor_advice: Schedule an appointment if you notice rapid growth, color changes, or persistent pain.
Age Spots.symptoms: Variable depending on the stage; often involves redness, texture changes, or discomfort.
Age Spots.prevention: Maintain good skin hygiene and protect yourself from environmental triggers.
Age Spots.locations: Can occur on various parts of the body depending on the condition.
Age Spots.diagnosis: Usually involves a clinical examination, sometimes supplemented by a biopsy or specific tests.
Age Spots.immediate_actions: Clean the area with mild soap and water. Document any changes with photos.
Age Spots.lifestyle: Maintain a healthy diet and skin-care routine. Avoid known allergens.

Alopecia Areata.advice: An autoimmune condition where the immune system attacks hair follicles. Hair often regrows but may fall out again.
Alopecia Areata.cautions: Hair loss can be sudden. Consult a dermatologist for treatment options as early intervention is best.
Alopecia Areata.complications: Total scalp hair loss (alopecia totalis) or total body hair loss (alopecia universalis).
Alopecia Areata.solutions: Corticosteroid injections, topical immunotherapy, or Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors.
Alopecia Areata.doctor_advice: See a specialist if you notice circular patches of hair loss or thinning on the scalp or body.
Alopecia Areata.symptoms: Patchy hair loss, 'exclamation point' hairs at patch edges, and occasional itching or pain.
Alopecia Areata.prevention: No known prevention as it is an autoimmune disorder.
Alopecia Areata.locations: Scalp, beard area, eyebrows, and eyelashes.
Alopecia Areata.diagnosis: Clinical examination and sometimes a skin biopsy or blood tests for other autoimmune diseases.
Alopecia Areata.immediate_actions: Protect the bald areas from sun exposure and avoid stress which may trigger flares.
Alopecia Areata.lifestyle: Manage stress through relaxation techniques; use cosmetic covers (wigs/hats) if desired.
visual_features: Smooth, round patches of hair loss
Exclamation point hairs (narrower at the base)

Athlete's Foot.advice: Fungal infection that thrives in warm, moist environments. Usually treated with topical antifungals.
Athlete's Foot.cautions: Highly contagious; avoid sharing towels or shoes. Don't go barefoot in public showers or locker rooms.
Athlete's Foot.complications: Spread to toenails (onychomycosis), secondary bacterial infections, or spread to hands (tinea manuum).
Athlete's Foot.solutions: Over-the-counter antifungal creams (terbinafine, clotrimazole), sprays, or powders.
Athlete's Foot.doctor_advice: See a doctor if the rash doesn't improve after 2 weeks of OTC treatment or if you have diabetes.
Athlete's Foot.symptoms: Itchy scaly rash, stinging or burning, cracked or peeling skin between toes.
Athlete's Foot.prevention: Keep feet dry (especially between toes), wear moisture-wicking socks, and use antifungal powder daily.
Athlete's Foot.locations: Between the toes, soles of the feet, and sides of the feet.
Athlete's Foot.diagnosis: Visual inspection; KOH skin scraping test if diagnosis is uncertain.
Athlete's Foot.immediate_actions: Apply an OTC antifungal cream and switch to clean, dry cotton socks.
Athlete's Foot.lifestyle: Alternate shoes daily to allow them to dry out. Wash socks in hot water.

Atopic Dermatitis.advice: Chronic inflammatory condition (Eczema). Key is maintaining the skin barrier through consistent moisturization.
Atopic Dermatitis.cautions: Avoid harsh soaps and hot water. Don't scratch, as it damages the skin barrier and leads to infection.
Atopic Dermatitis.complications: Secondary bacterial (Staph) or viral (Herpes) infections, skin thickening (lichenification).
Atopic Dermatitis.solutions: Topical corticosteroids, calcineurin inhibitors, antihistamines for itch, and biologics for severe cases.
Atopic Dermatitis.doctor_advice: Seek medical help if skin looks infected (pus, yellow crusts) or if itching prevents sleep.
Atopic Dermatitis.symptoms: Intense itching, dry skin, red to brownish-gray patches, thickened or scaly skin.
Atopic Dermatitis.prevention: Identify and avoid triggers (specific foods, pollen, dust, stress). Use lukewarm water for baths.
Atopic Dermatitis.locations: Folds of elbows, behind knees, face, neck, and wrists.
Atopic Dermatitis.diagnosis: Clinical history and physical examination; occasionally allergy patch testing.
Atopic Dermatitis.immediate_actions: Apply a thick, fragrance-free moisturizer (ointment or cream) and use a cool compress.
Atopic Dermatitis.lifestyle: Wear soft cotton clothing, avoid synthetic fabrics, and use a humidifier in winter.
visual_features: Oozing and crusting in acute phases

Basal Cell Carcinoma.advice: Most common skin cancer. Highly curable if caught early but can invade deep tissues if ignored.
Basal Cell Carcinoma.cautions: Do not attempt home remedies. Surgical intervention is usually necessary.
Basal Cell Carcinoma.complications: Local tissue destruction (skin, bone, cartilage), recurrence in same area, and risk of other skin cancers.
Basal Cell Carcinoma.solutions: Mohs surgery, surgical excision, cryosurgery, or topical chemotherapy.
Basal Cell Carcinoma.doctor_advice: Consult a dermatologist for any sore that bleeds, heals, and returns, or any new pearly bump.
Basal Cell Carcinoma.symptoms: Pearly or waxy bump, flat scarlike lesion, or a bleeding sore that doesn't heal.
Basal Cell Carcinoma.prevention: Strict sun protection, annual full-body skin exams, and avoidance of tanning beds.
Basal Cell Carcinoma.locations: Head, neck, and other sun-exposed areas like arms and legs.
Basal Cell Carcinoma.diagnosis: Visual skin exam followed by a shave or punch biopsy.
Basal Cell Carcinoma.immediate_actions: Take a photo for reference and schedule a dermatology appointment immediately.
Basal Cell Carcinoma.lifestyle: Avoid peak sun hours (10 AM - 4 PM) and wear UPF 50+ protective clothing.

Bed Sores.advice: Pressure ulcers caused by prolonged pressure on the skin. Common in people with medical conditions that limit their ability to change positions.
Bed Sores.cautions: Can quickly progress to deep tissue damage. Prevent by repositioning every 2 hours.
Bed Sores.complications: Sepsis, bone and joint infections (osteomyelitis), and cellulitis.
Bed Sores.solutions: Pressure-relieving surfaces (special cushions/mattresses), wound cleaning, and sometimes surgical debridement.
Bed Sores.doctor_advice: Consult a wound care specialist immediately for any skin breakdown in immobile patients.
Bed Sores.symptoms: Unusual changes in skin color or texture, swelling, pus-like draining, and skin that feels cooler or warmer than other areas.
Bed Sores.prevention: Frequent repositioning, skin inspections, and maintaining good nutrition/hydration.
Bed Sores.locations: Bony areas such as heels, ankles, hips, and tailbone.
Bed Sores.diagnosis: Visual inspection by a healthcare provider; staging from Stage 1 (mild) to Stage 4 (deepest).
Bed Sores.immediate_actions: Relieve pressure from the affected area immediately and keep it clean and dry.
Bed Sores.lifestyle: Use pressure-redistributing cushions and maintain a high-protein diet for skin healing.
visual_features: Non-blanchable erythema (redness that doesn't turn white when pressed)

Boils.advice: A painful, pus-filled bump under the skin caused by infected hair follicles (Staph bacteria).
Boils.cautions: Never squeeze or lance a boil yourself; this can push the infection deeper into the skin.
Boils.complications: Carbuncles (cluster of boils), scarring, and blood poisoning (sepsis) in rare cases.
Boils.solutions: Warm compresses to encourage drainage, and incision and drainage (I&D) by a professional.
Boils.doctor_advice: See a doctor if the boil is on your face, is extremely painful, or causes a fever.
Boils.symptoms: A red, painful lump that grows larger and develops a white or yellow tip (point).
Boils.prevention: Wash hands regularly, keep wounds covered, and don't share personal items like towels.
Boils.locations: Face, neck, armpits, thighs, and buttocks.
Boils.diagnosis: Clinical examination; a culture of the pus may be taken if the infection is recurrent.
Boils.immediate_actions: Apply a warm, moist compress for 10-15 minutes several times a day.
Boils.lifestyle: Maintain good overall hygiene and use antibacterial soap if prone to recurrences.
visual_features: Presence of a central pustule or 'head'

Bullous Pemphigoid.advice: A rare autoimmune condition causing large, fluid-filled blisters. Most common in elderly patients.
Bullous Pemphigoid.cautions: Do not pop the blisters as it increases the risk of infection. Requires systemic treatment.
Bullous Pemphigoid.complications: Sepsis from infected blisters, dehydration, and side effects from long-term steroid use.
Bullous Pemphigoid.solutions: High-potency topical steroids, oral corticosteroids (prednisone), or steroid-sparing immunosuppressants.
Bullous Pemphigoid.doctor_advice: Consult a dermatologist urgently if you develop large blisters on a red or normal skin base.
Bullous Pemphigoid.symptoms: Intense itching followed by large, tense blisters that don't rupture easily.
Bullous Pemphigoid.prevention: Not preventable; triggered by a malfunction in the immune system.
Bullous Pemphigoid.locations: Lower abdomen, groin, upper thighs, and arms.
Bullous Pemphigoid.diagnosis: Skin biopsy for histopathology and direct immunofluorescence (DIF).
Bullous Pemphigoid.immediate_actions: Avoid irritating the skin and schedule a specialist appointment immediately.
Bullous Pemphigoid.lifestyle: Maintain good nutrition and use non-adherent dressings for ruptured blisters.
visual_features: Nikolsky sign is negative (skin doesn't peel when rubbed)

Candidiasis.advice: Treatment depends on the site. Oral thrush or vaginal yeast infections often require specific antifungal medications.
Candidiasis.cautions: Immune-compromised individuals are at higher risk for invasive candidiasis, which is a medical emergency.
Candidiasis.complications: Systemic infection (candidemia), endocarditis, or organ damage in severe cases.
Candidiasis.solutions: Topical antifungals for skin/mucosa; systemic antifungals (echinocandins) for invasive cases.
Candidiasis.doctor_advice: Seek medical help if you have a persistent fever, difficulty swallowing, or if you are at high risk for infection.
Candidiasis.symptoms: Creamy white patches (oral), intense itching and white discharge (vaginal), or itchy red rash in skin folds.
Candidiasis.prevention: Maintain good hygiene, keep skin folds dry, and manage underlying conditions like diabetes.
Candidiasis.locations: Mouth, vagina, skin folds (intertriginous areas), or systemic.
Candidiasis.diagnosis: Clinical examination, KOH prep, or fungal culture.
Candidiasis.immediate_actions: Keep the affected area dry. Avoid using irritants or scented products.
Candidiasis.lifestyle: Wear breathable cotton clothing and maintain a balanced diet.

Cellulitis.advice: Cellulitis is a serious bacterial infection that requires prompt antibiotic treatment to prevent complications.
Cellulitis.cautions: Do not delay treatment. If redness spreads rapidly or you develop a fever, seek emergency care.
Cellulitis.complications: Sepsis, necrotizing fasciitis, osteomyelitis, or permanent tissue damage.
Cellulitis.solutions: Oral or intravenous antibiotics are necessary. Elevate the affected limb to reduce swelling.
Cellulitis.doctor_advice: Go to an emergency room if you have a high fever, red streaks spreading from the area, or severe pain.
Cellulitis.symptoms: Rapidly spreading redness, warmth, swelling, pain, and sometimes fever or chills.
Cellulitis.prevention: Treat skin injuries promptly, maintain good hygiene, and moisturize dry/cracked skin.
Cellulitis.locations: Most common on the lower legs, but can occur anywhere.
Cellulitis.diagnosis: Clinical appearance and medical history; blood tests or cultures may be needed.
Cellulitis.immediate_actions: Keep the area clean. Mark the borders of redness with a pen to track spreading.
Cellulitis.lifestyle: Protect skin from injury and manage underlying conditions like lymphedema.

Chickenpox.advice: Viral infection (Varicella) characterized by itchy blisters. Highly contagious until all blisters have scabbed.
Chickenpox.cautions: Do not give aspirin to children with chickenpox (risk of Reye's syndrome). Keep away from pregnant women.
Chickenpox.complications: Bacterial skin infections, pneumonia, encephalitis, and shingles (later in life).
Chickenpox.solutions: Calamine lotion, oatmeal baths, cool compresses, and antiviral meds for high-risk individuals.
Chickenpox.doctor_advice: Call doctor if fever lasts >4 days, is >102°F, or if child has trouble breathing or walking.
Chickenpox.symptoms: Fever, headache, fatigue, followed by crops of itchy fluid-filled blisters that scab over.
Chickenpox.prevention: Varicella vaccine is highly effective. Isolate from others to prevent spread.
Chickenpox.locations: Starts on chest, back and face, then spreads to the rest of the body.
Chickenpox.diagnosis: Clinical appearance of the rash; occasionally viral culture or PCR swab.
Chickenpox.immediate_actions: Isolate the patient. Use calamine lotion for itch. Trim fingernails to prevent scratch injury.
Chickenpox.lifestyle: Stay home from school/work. Rest and maintain fluid intake to prevent dehydration.
visual_features: Crusted lesions present alongside fresh blisters

Cold Sores.advice: Small fluid-filled blisters caused by Herpes Simplex Virus Type 1. Very contagious through direct contact.
Cold Sores.cautions: Avoid kissing or sharing utensils during an outbreak. Don't touch eyes after touching a sore.
Cold Sores.complications: Spread to eyes (herpetic keratitis), spread to other areas (whitlow on fingers), secondary infection.
Cold Sores.solutions: Antiviral creams (docosanol), prescription oral antivirals (acyclovir), and pain relief patches.
Cold Sores.doctor_advice: See a doctor if sores don't heal in 2 weeks, if you have frequent outbreaks, or if eyes become irritated.
Cold Sores.symptoms: Tingling/itching sensation before blisters appear, followed by a cluster of small painful blisters.
Cold Sores.prevention: Manage stress, avoid excessive sun, and don't share personal items with infected individuals.
Cold Sores.locations: On or around the lips, sometimes on the nose or cheeks.
Cold Sores.diagnosis: Physical examination; viral culture or PCR test from a blister swab.
Cold Sores.immediate_actions: Apply an antiviral cream at the first sign of tingling. Wash hands thoroughly.
Cold Sores.lifestyle: Use sunblock on lips if triggered by UV. Get adequate rest to support the immune system.

Contact Dermatitis.advice: Skin inflammation triggered by substance contact. Can be Irritant (soap/solvents) or Allergic (nickel/perfume).
Contact Dermatitis.cautions: Stop using the suspected product immediately. Don't use hot water on the area as it increases inflammation.
Contact Dermatitis.complications: Secondary bacterial infection, chronic skin thickening, and persistent itching.
Contact Dermatitis.solutions: Identify/avoid toxin, topical steroid creams, oral antihistamines, and cool compresses.
Contact Dermatitis.doctor_advice: See professional if rash is severe, involves eyes/genitals, or covers more than 25% of body.
Contact Dermatitis.symptoms: Red itchy rash, dry scaly skin (irritant), or blisters and oozing (allergic).
Contact Dermatitis.prevention: Use fragrance-free products, wear protective gloves, and wash skin quickly after contact with allergens.
Contact Dermatitis.locations: Directly on the area that touched the substance (hands are most common).
Contact Dermatitis.diagnosis: Clinical history; patch testing for persistent or chronic cases.
Contact Dermatitis.immediate_actions: Wash the area with cool water and mild soap to remove any remaining triggers.
Contact Dermatitis.lifestyle: Switch to hypoallergenic laundry detergents and soaps. Avoid cheap jewelry if nickel sensitive.

Cradle Cap.advice: A common, harmless skin condition in infants (infantile seborrheic dermatitis) causing crusty or oily scales.
Cradle Cap.cautions: Do not pick or scrape the scales as it can cause irritation or infection.
Cradle Cap.complications: Secondary bacterial or fungal infection in the skin folds.
Cradle Cap.solutions: Frequent hair washing with mild baby shampoo and gentle brushing of the scales.
Cradle Cap.doctor_advice: See a pediatrician if the rash spreads, becomes very red, or looks infected (oozing).
Cradle Cap.symptoms: Thick, yellow, greasy scales or crusts on the scalp; sometimes mild redness.
Cradle Cap.prevention: Regular hair washing and gentle scalp massage to prevent scale buildup.
Cradle Cap.locations: Scalp is most common; can also appear on ears, eyelids, and nose.
Cradle Cap.diagnosis: Diagnosed by its characteristic 'greasy' appearance on an infant's scalp.
Cradle Cap.immediate_actions: Apply a small amount of baby oil to the scalp for 10 minutes to soften scales before washing.
Cradle Cap.lifestyle: Maintain a gentle hygiene routine and use soft-bristled baby brushes.
visual_features: Adherent crusts that may flake off

Cysts.advice: Fluid-filled sacs (epidermoid or sebaceous cysts) that are usually slow-growing and painless.
Cysts.cautions: Do not attempt to pop or drain them as they often return unless the entire sac is removed.
Cysts.complications: Rupture (causing inflammation), infection (abscess), and cosmetic concern.
Cysts.solutions: Monitoring, corticosteroid injections to reduce inflammation, or surgical excision.
Cysts.doctor_advice: Consult a doctor if the cyst becomes painful, red, or grows rapidly.
Cysts.symptoms: A small, round bump under the skin, sometimes with a tiny blackhead (pore) at the center.
Cysts.prevention: No reliable prevention; avoid trauma to the skin which can trigger their formation.
Cysts.locations: Face, neck, trunk, and behind the ears.
Cysts.diagnosis: Visual exam; ultrasound or biopsy if the diagnosis is uncertain.
Cysts.immediate_actions: Leave the bump alone; if it becomes red and painful, apply a warm compress.
Cysts.lifestyle: Avoid tight clothing over the area to prevent irritation and potential rupture.

Dandruff.advice: A mild form of seborrheic dermatitis. Involves flaking of skin on the scalp.
Dandruff.cautions: Don't scratch the scalp as it can lead to bleeding or bacterial infection. Manage stress as it can flare up.
Dandruff.complications: Scalp irritation, secondary infection if scratched, and social embarrassment.
Dandruff.solutions: Anti-dandruff shampoos (zinc pyrithione, ketoconazole, selenium sulfide), and regular hair washing.
Dandruff.doctor_advice: Consult a doctor if scalp is very red/swollen or if OTC dandruff shampoos don't help after 1 month.
Dandruff.symptoms: White or yellowish flakes on scalp/shoulders, itchy scalp, scaly/crusty scalp.
Dandruff.prevention: Regular shampooing, managing stress, and reducing hair product buildup.
Dandruff.locations: Scalp, hairline, eyebrows, and behind the ears.
Dandruff.diagnosis: Visual examination of the scalp and flakes.
Dandruff.immediate_actions: Purchase a medicated anti-dandruff shampoo and use it as directed (leave on for 5 mins).
Dandruff.lifestyle: Get a little sunlight (can help with Malassezia) and maintain good scalp hygiene.

Dermatofibroma.advice: Common, benign (non-cancerous) fibrous growths that often feel like a firm nodule under the skin.
Dermatofibroma.cautions: Harmless; they usually don't need treatment unless they are itchy or cosmetically bothering.
Dermatofibroma.complications: Minor irritation from shaving or clothing; no malignant potential.
Dermatofibroma.solutions: Cryotherapy to flatten the lesion or surgical excision if necessary.
Dermatofibroma.doctor_advice: Consult a dermatologist if you notice a new, changing, or bleeding firm bump.
Dermatofibroma.symptoms: A firm, small, raised bump that may be itchy or tender. Often brownish or reddish.
Dermatofibroma.prevention: No prevention; thought to be a reaction to minor skin injuries like insect bites.
Dermatofibroma.locations: Most common on the lower legs.
Dermatofibroma.diagnosis: Clinical exam; the 'dimple sign' (lesion puckers when pinched) is characteristic.
Dermatofibroma.immediate_actions: Avoid picking at the bump; document if it changes in size or color.
Dermatofibroma.lifestyle: Be careful when shaving over the area; ignore it if it is stable and asymptomatic.

Dermatomyositis.advice: An inflammatory disease marked by muscle weakness and a distinctive skin rash.
Dermatomyositis.cautions: Requires whole-body evaluation. In adults, it can sometimes be associated with internal cancers.
Dermatomyositis.complications: Interstitial lung disease, calcinosis, and muscle permanent weakness.
Dermatomyositis.doctor_advice: Consult a rheumatologist or dermatologist if you have a purple rash on eyelids and muscle fatigue.
Dermatomyositis.symptoms: Purple or red rash on eyelids, knuckles, and chest; difficulty climbing stairs or lifting objects.
Dermatomyositis.prevention: No known prevention; focus on management and early detection of complications.
Dermatomyositis.locations: Upper eyelids (heliotrope rash), knuckles (Gottron's papules), and upper back/shoulders (Shawl sign).
Dermatomyositis.diagnosis: Blood tests (CK levels), muscle biopsy, and skin biopsy.
Dermatomyositis.immediate_actions: Avoid sun exposure as it can flare the skin symptoms; rest weakened muscles.
Dermatomyositis.lifestyle: Sun protection is critical. Follow a gradual exercise program once inflammation is controlled.

Diaper Rash.advice: An irritant contact dermatitis in the diaper area caused by moisture, friction, and urine/feces.
Diaper Rash.cautions: If the rash has bright red spots or 'satellite' lesions, it may be a yeast infection (Candida).
Diaper Rash.complications: Secondary yeast infection and skin erosions.
Diaper Rash.solutions: Barrier creams (zinc oxide), frequent diaper changes, and 'air time' without a diaper.
Diaper Rash.doctor_advice: See a pediatrician if the rash lasts more than 3 days, bleeds, or oozes pus.
Diaper Rash.symptoms: Bright red, tender skin in the diaper area; baby may be fussy during diaper changes.
Diaper Rash.prevention: Change diapers frequently, use fragrance-free wipes, and apply barrier cream at every change.
Diaper Rash.locations: Buttocks, thighs, and genital area of infants.
Diaper Rash.diagnosis: Visual inspection by a parent or healthcare provider.
Diaper Rash.immediate_actions: Gently clean the area with plain water and pat dry. Apply a thick layer of zinc oxide cream.
Diaper Rash.lifestyle: Use high-absorbency diapers and avoid overly tight diapering.
visual_features: Possible satellite papules if yeast is present

Dry Skin.advice: Also known as xerosis; it occurs when the skin lacks moisture in its outer layer.
Dry Skin.cautions: Extremely dry skin can crack, providing an entry point for bacteria and leading to infection.
Dry Skin.solutions: Ceramide-rich moisturizers, urea-based creams, and avoidance of harsh soaps.
Dry Skin.doctor_advice: Consult a doctor if the skin is so dry that it bleeds or prevents you from sleeping.
Dry Skin.symptoms: Skin tightness, flaking, fine lines, and itching.
Dry Skin.prevention: Short, lukewarm showers; apply moisturizer to damp skin; use a humidifier.
Dry Skin.locations: Commonly legs, arms, and hands, but can occur anywhere.
Dry Skin.diagnosis: Clinical examination based on visual appearance and patient symptoms.
Dry Skin.immediate_actions: Switch to a gentle, soap-free cleanser and apply a thick ointment-based moisturizer.
Dry Skin.lifestyle: Keep hydrated and avoid environmental irritants like cold wind and low-humidity air.

Dyshidrosis.advice: A type of eczema (dyshidrotic eczema) causing tiny, fluid-filled blisters on the palms and fingers.
Dyshidrosis.cautions: Blisters are often intensely itchy. Scratching can lead to painful cracks and infection.
Dyshidrosis.complications: Secondary bacterial infection (Staph) and significant hand discomfort.
Dyshidrosis.solutions: High-potency topical steroids, cool compresses, and avoiding contact with allergens/irritants.
Dyshidrosis.doctor_advice: See a dermatologist for recurrent episodes or if the blisters become infected (pus/pain).
Dyshidrosis.symptoms: Very small, deep-seated blisters ('tapioca-like'), burning sensation, and intense itching.
Dyshidrosis.prevention: Identify and avoid triggers such as nickel, cobalt, or excessive moisture/sweating.
Dyshidrosis.locations: Edges of fingers, palms of hands, and soles of feet.
Dyshidrosis.diagnosis: Diagnosed by clinical presentation; skin testing for allergies if chronic.
Dyshidrosis.immediate_actions: Apply a cool compress for 15 minutes and avoid use of irritating soaps/detergents.
Dyshidrosis.lifestyle: Wear cotton gloves under vinyl gloves for wet work; keep hands dry and well-moisturized.
visual_features: Erythema and scaling in later stages

Ecthyma.advice: A deep-seated bacterial skin infection that causes painful ulcers with thick crusts.
Ecthyma.cautions: A more severe form of impetigo; it penetrates into the lower layers of the skin.
Ecthyma.complications: Scarring (unlike superficial impetigo), cellulitis, and lymphangitis.
Ecthyma.solutions: Prescription oral antibiotics and topical antibiotic ointments (mupirocin).
Ecthyma.doctor_advice: Consult a doctor for any sore that turns into a deep, painful hole in the skin with a crust.
Ecthyma.symptoms: Sores that look like deep ulcers, often with a 'punched-out' appearance and a thick grayish-yellow crust.
Ecthyma.prevention: Prompt treatment of minor skin injuries and maintaining good personal hygiene.
Ecthyma.locations: Commonly on the shins and feet.
Ecthyma.diagnosis: Visual inspection; culture of the ulcer base may be needed to identify the bacteria.
Ecthyma.immediate_actions: Cover the area and see a doctor for prescription medication.
Ecthyma.lifestyle: Keep the area clean, avoid sharing towels, and finish the full course of antibiotics.

Eczema.advice: A term for several types of skin inflammation (most commonly atopic dermatitis) causing dry, itchy skin.
Eczema.cautions: Scratching the 'itch that rashes' can break the skin and lead to bacterial infections.
Eczema.complications: Bacterial infections (Staph), eczema herpeticum (viral infection), and thickening of the skin.
Eczema.solutions: Topical corticosteroids, calcineurin inhibitors, and consistent use of fragrance-free emollients.
Eczema.doctor_advice: Consult a dermatologist for a personalized management plan and to identify potential triggers.
Eczema.symptoms: Intense itching, red to brownish-gray patches, and small raised bumps that may leak fluid.
Eczema.prevention: Identify and avoid triggers like harsh soaps, certain fabrics, and allergens.
Eczema.diagnosis: Based on skin appearance and personal/family history of allergies or asthma.
Eczema.immediate_actions: Stop using scented products and apply a heavy cream after bathing.
Eczema.lifestyle: Take short, lukewarm baths; wear soft cotton clothing; and manage stress.

Epidermolysis Bullosa.advice: A group of rare genetic conditions that cause the skin to be very fragile and to blister easily (often called 'butterfly skin').
Epidermolysis Bullosa.cautions: Blisters can form from minor friction, heat, or rubbing. Requires specialized wound care.
Epidermolysis Bullosa.complications: Sepsis, anemia, malnutrition (from mouth blisters), and skin cancer (SCC) at a young age.
Epidermolysis Bullosa.solutions: Protective dressings, pain management, and surgical release of contracted digits (pseudosyndactyly).
Epidermolysis Bullosa.doctor_advice: Requires lifelong care from a multidisciplinary team including dermatologists and wound care nurses.
Epidermolysis Bullosa.symptoms: Widespread blisters, fragile skin that shears easily, and thickening of the skin on palms and soles.
Epidermolysis Bullosa.prevention: Genetic condition; avoid skin trauma and keep the skin cool.
Epidermolysis Bullosa.locations: Anywhere on the skin and mucous membranes.
Epidermolysis Bullosa.diagnosis: Skin biopsy for immunofluorescence mapping or genetic testing.
Epidermolysis Bullosa.immediate_actions: Use non-adherent bandages and never pull at detached skin.
Epidermolysis Bullosa.lifestyle: Wear soft, seamless clothing and avoid activities with high risk of skin contact or friction.
visual_features: Milia (small white bumps) at site of healed blisters
Scarring and fusion of digits in severe types

Erysipelas.advice: A superficial bacterial skin infection (usually Strep) characterized by a fiery red, well-defined rash.
Erysipelas.cautions: Can quickly spread and lead to high fever and chills. Requires prompt antibiotic treatment.
Erysipelas.complications: Lymphedema, abscess formation, and necrotizing fasciitis if not treated.
Erysipelas.solutions: Oral or intravenous antibiotics (penicillin) and limb elevation.
Erysipelas.doctor_advice: Seek immediate medical attention for a fast-spreading, painful red rash with fever.
Erysipelas.symptoms: Intense redness, warmth, swelling, and a clear 'raised border' between infected and normal skin.
Erysipelas.prevention: Promptly clean and treat minor cuts, and manage underlying conditions like lymphedema or athlete's foot.
Erysipelas.locations: Most common on the legs and face.
Erysipelas.diagnosis: Clinical examination based on the sharp demarcation of the rash; blood cultures if severe.
Erysipelas.immediate_actions: See a doctor immediately; elevate the affected limb to reduce swelling.
Erysipelas.lifestyle: Maintain consistent skin hygiene and keep skin well-moisturized to prevent cracks.

Erythema Multiforme.advice: A hypersensitivity reaction often triggered by infections, most commonly the herpes simplex virus.
Erythema Multiforme.cautions: May be confused with more severe conditions like Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS).
Erythema Multiforme.complications: Recurrence (common) and potential for involvement of mucous membranes.
Erythema Multiforme.solutions: Treating the underlying infection, topical steroids, and antihistamines for itching.
Erythema Multiforme.doctor_advice: Consult a dermatologist if you develop target-like red spots on your hands or body.
Erythema Multiforme.symptoms: Characteristic 'target' or 'bullseye' lesions with a dark center, a pale ring, and an outer red ring.
Erythema Multiforme.prevention: Antiviral drugs (acyclovir) can prevent recurrences if HSV is the known trigger.
Erythema Multiforme.locations: Hands, feet, and limbs; can sometimes affect the mouth.
Erythema Multiforme.diagnosis: Diagnosed by the unique target appearance of the skin lesions.
Erythema Multiforme.immediate_actions: Avoid triggers and use cool compresses for comfort; see a doctor for formal diagnosis.
Erythema Multiforme.lifestyle: Document any new medications or recent infections that may have triggered the rash.

Erythema Nodosum.advice: An inflammatory condition characterized by painful, red nodules under the skin, usually on the shins.
Erythema Nodosum.cautions: Often a sign of an underlying condition like infection (Strep), pregnancy, or drug reaction.
Erythema Nodosum.complications: Chronic or recurrent nodules; underlying disease progression if not identified.
Erythema Nodosum.solutions: Rest, NSAIDs for pain, and treating the underlying cause.
Erythema Nodosum.doctor_advice: Consult a doctor to identify the trigger for the nodules.
Erythema Nodosum.symptoms: Tender, warm, red bumps that feel like bruises. Often accompanied by fever or joint pain.
Erythema Nodosum.prevention: Manage systemic health and promptly treat infections that could trigger inflammation.
Erythema Nodosum.diagnosis: Physical examination and blood tests/imaging to look for an underlying trigger.
Erythema Nodosum.immediate_actions: Rest and elevate the legs to reduce pain and swelling.
Erythema Nodosum.lifestyle: Avoid long periods of standing while nodules are active.
visual_features: Bruise-like color changes as they heal (purple/green)

Folliculitis.advice: Most cases are mild and resolve with self-care. Persistent or severe cases may need medical attention.
Folliculitis.cautions: Avoid shaving the affected area and do not squeeze or pop the bumps.
Folliculitis.complications: Boils (furunculosis), permanent hair loss, or scarring (keloids).
Folliculitis.solutions: Warm compresses, antibacterial washes, or topical/oral antibiotics for severe cases.
Folliculitis.doctor_advice: Consult a doctor if the infection spreads, returns frequently, or causes significant pain.
Folliculitis.symptoms: Small red bumps or white-headed pimples around hair follicles, itching, or tenderness.
Folliculitis.prevention: Avoid tight clothing, shave carefully with a clean blade, and maintain hygiene in pools/hot tubs.
Folliculitis.locations: Anywhere hair grows, especially the beard area, scalp, and thighs.
Folliculitis.diagnosis: Based on skin appearance; a swab may be taken for bacterial or fungal testing.
Folliculitis.immediate_actions: Apply a warm, moist compress to the area. Stop hair removal temporarily.
Folliculitis.lifestyle: Wear loose clothing and use clean razors and shaving cream.

Fungal Infections.advice: Common infections caused by various fungi (dermatophytes or yeasts) that thrive in warm, moist areas.
Fungal Infections.cautions: Often contagious; avoid sharing clothes or towels with infected individuals.
Fungal Infections.complications: Secondary bacterial infection (cellulitis) from skin maceration or scratching.
Fungal Infections.solutions: Topical antifungal creams (clotrimazole, terbinafine) and keeping the area dry.
Fungal Infections.doctor_advice: Consult a doctor if the infection covers a large area or doesn't improve with OTC creams.
Fungal Infections.symptoms: Red, itchy, scaly rash, sometimes with a clear center (ring-like) or small blisters.
Fungal Infections.prevention: Keep skin clean and dry, wear breathable clothing, and use anti-fungal powder in shoes.
Fungal Infections.locations: Groin (jock itch), feet (athlete's foot), and body (ringworm).
Fungal Infections.diagnosis: Visual inspection; KOH prep skin scraping to see fungal elements under a microscope.
Fungal Infections.immediate_actions: Keep the area dry and apply an over-the-counter antifungal cream.
Fungal Infections.lifestyle: Change socks and underwear daily and use separate towels for infected areas.

Fungal Nail Infection.advice: A slow-growing infection (onychomycosis) that causes nails to become thickened, brittle, and discolored.
Fungal Nail Infection.cautions: Hard to treat with topical medications alone; often requires long-term oral treatment.
Fungal Nail Infection.complications: Total nail destruction, pain while walking, and spread to other nails.
Fungal Nail Infection.solutions: Oral antifungal tablets (terbinafine), medicated nail lacquers, or surgical nail removal.
Fungal Nail Infection.doctor_advice: See a doctor if the nail is painful, very thick, or if you have diabetes.
Fungal Nail Infection.symptoms: Thickened, yellow or brown nails, crumbly or brittle texture, and debris under the nail.
Fungal Nail Infection.prevention: Keep feet dry, wear flip-flops in shared showers, and use breathable footwear.
Fungal Nail Infection.locations: Toenails are most common, but can affect fingernails.
Fungal Nail Infection.diagnosis: Clinical appearance; confirmed by nail clipping culture or PAS stain.
Fungal Nail Infection.immediate_actions: Keep nails trimmed short and avoid using communal showers without footwear.
Fungal Nail Infection.lifestyle: Don't share nail clippers and use antifungal sprays in shoes.
visual_features: Yellow/white streaking in the nail plate

Granuloma Annulare.advice: A benign, chronic skin condition that causes raised, reddish or skin-colored bumps in a ring pattern.
Granuloma Annulare.cautions: Harmless and not contagious; often mistaken for ringworm because of the ring shape.
Granuloma Annulare.complications: Minor cosmetic concern; usually resolves on its own without scarring.
Granuloma Annulare.solutions: Observation (often self-resolving), topical or intralesional steroids, and cryotherapy.
Granuloma Annulare.doctor_advice: See a dermatologist for a firm diagnosis as it can resemble other skin conditions.
Granuloma Annulare.symptoms: Small, firm, smooth bumps that expand into a ring with a sunken or clear center. No scaling.
Granuloma Annulare.prevention: No known prevention; sometimes triggered by minor skin trauma or medications.
Granuloma Annulare.locations: Backs of hands, feet, elbows, and knees.
Granuloma Annulare.diagnosis: Visual inspection is often sufficient; skin biopsy can confirm for atypical cases.
Granuloma Annulare.immediate_actions: Reassurance that it is benign; use a mild moisturizer if the area is dry.
Granuloma Annulare.lifestyle: Avoid aggressive scrubbing of the area; wait for it to resolve naturally.

Hand, Foot, and Mouth Disease.advice: A common viral illness in children characterized by fever, mouth sores, and a skin rash with blisters.
Hand, Foot, and Mouth Disease.cautions: Highly contagious through saliva, blister fluid, or feces. Keep child home while blisters are present.
Hand, Foot, and Mouth Disease.complications: Dehydration (if mouth sores make swallowing difficult) and rare viral meningitis.
Hand, Foot, and Mouth Disease.solutions: Pain relief (acetaminophen), hydration, and numbing mouth sprays.
Hand, Foot, and Mouth Disease.doctor_advice: Consult a pediatrician if your child stops drinking or if the fever lasts more than 3 days.
Hand, Foot, and Mouth Disease.symptoms: Small blisters on palms, soles, and buttocks; painful ulcers in the mouth and throat.
Hand, Foot, and Mouth Disease.prevention: Frequent hand washing and disinfecting shared toys/surfaces.
Hand, Foot, and Mouth Disease.locations: Hands, feet, and inside the mouth.
Hand, Foot, and Mouth Disease.diagnosis: Diagnosed by the unique distribution of blisters and clinical symptoms.
Hand, Foot, and Mouth Disease.immediate_actions: Encourage fluids (popsicles) and manage fever with weight-appropriate medication.
Hand, Foot, and Mouth Disease.lifestyle: Wait until sores have dried and fever has ended before returning to daycare/school.
visual_features: Small, oval gray vesicles on a red base
Symmetrical involvement of hands and feet

Heat Rash.advice: Also called miliaria; it occurs when sweat ducts are blocked, trapping sweat beneath the skin.
Heat Rash.cautions: Can cause intense stinging or itching. Avoid heavy creams that can block pores further.
Heat Rash.solutions: Cooling the skin, calamine lotion, and Wearing loose, breathable cotton clothing.
Heat Rash.doctor_advice: See a doctor if the skin develops pus, increased swelling, or if you feel unwell (fever).
Heat Rash.symptoms: Clusters of small, red, prickly bumps or tiny clear blisters in areas of sweating.
Heat Rash.prevention: Stay in cool environments, wear loose clothing, and avoid heavy body oils.
Heat Rash.locations: Neck, shoulders, chest, and skin folds.
Heat Rash.diagnosis: Based on the appearance of the rash in the setting of heat or excessive sweating.
Heat Rash.immediate_actions: Take a cool bath and move to an air-conditioned or fan-cooled room.
Heat Rash.lifestyle: Sleep in a cool room and choose lightweight fabrics like linen or cotton.

Hemangioma.advice: A benign (non-cancerous) bright red birthmark (strawberry mark) made of extra blood vessels in the skin.
Hemangioma.cautions: Rapid growth in the first few months is common, followed by slow disappearance (involution) over years.
Hemangioma.complications: Ulceration (bleeding/pain) and potential vision/breathing issues if near eyes or airway.
Hemangioma.solutions: Most need no treatment. Options include oral beta-blockers (propranolol) to shrink them if necessary.
Hemangioma.doctor_advice: See a specialist for any hemangioma that is growing fast, ulcers, or is near a vital organ (eye/mouth).
Hemangioma.symptoms: A bright red, spongy-looking nodule that appears in the first few weeks of life.
Hemangioma.prevention: No known prevention; they are a common vascular birthmark in infants.
Hemangioma.diagnosis: Diagnosed by clinical appearance and history of rapid neonatal growth.
Hemangioma.immediate_actions: Consult a pediatrician to decide if the lesion requires monitoring or early treatment.
Hemangioma.lifestyle: Keep the area protected from trauma; use a barrier ointment if it starts to ulcerate.
visual_features: Gradual grayish fading as it involutes

Herpes Simplex.advice: Common viral infection causing small, painful blisters (cold sores or genital herpes) caused by HSV-1 or HSV-2.
Herpes Simplex.cautions: Highly contagious during an outbreak; avoid skin-to-skin contact and sharing items like lip balm.
Herpes Simplex.complications: Recurrent outbreaks, eye infections (herpetic keratitis), and rare but severe encephalitis.
Herpes Simplex.solutions: Antiviral medications (acyclovir, valacyclovir) to reduce duration and severity of outbreaks.
Herpes Simplex.doctor_advice: Consult a doctor for frequent outbreaks or if the sores are near your eyes.
Herpes Simplex.symptoms: Tingling or burning sensation followed by clusters of small fluid-filled blisters on a red base.
Herpes Simplex.prevention: Avoid contact with active sores; use sun protection as UV light can trigger cold sores.
Herpes Simplex.locations: Lips, mouth, genitals, and sometimes fingers (herpetic whitlow).
Herpes Simplex.diagnosis: Clinical appearance; confirmed by viral swab (PCR) of the lesion.
Herpes Simplex.immediate_actions: Avoid touching the sores and start antiviral treatment at the first sign of tingling.
Herpes Simplex.lifestyle: Manage stress and maintain a healthy immune system to prevent recurrences.
visual_features: Grouped vesicles on an erythematous base
Scabbing or crusting as blisters heal

Hidradenitis Suppurativa.advice: A chronic skin condition causing painful bumps and tunnels under the skin, usually in areas where skin rubs together.
Hidradenitis Suppurativa.cautions: Often mistaken for recurring boils. Requires long-term management by a specialist.
Hidradenitis Suppurativa.complications: Chronic drainage, scarring, sinus tracts (tunnels), and restricted movement.
Hidradenitis Suppurativa.solutions: Topical and oral antibiotics, biologics (adalimumab), and in severe cases, surgical debridement.
Hidradenitis Suppurativa.doctor_advice: See a dermatologist for any recurring, painful nodules in the armpits or groin.
Hidradenitis Suppurativa.symptoms: Painful bumps, abscesses that rupture, and leaking fluid with an odor.
Hidradenitis Suppurativa.prevention: Maintain a healthy weight and quit smoking, as these are major risk factors.
Hidradenitis Suppurativa.locations: Armpits, groin, under the breasts, and between the buttocks.
Hidradenitis Suppurativa.diagnosis: Clinical history and physical exam; based on the location and recurrence of nodules.
Hidradenitis Suppurativa.immediate_actions: Apply warm compresses to aid drainage and avoid shaving the affected areas.
Hidradenitis Suppurativa.lifestyle: Wear loose clothing, use antibacterial washes, and manage weight/smoking.

Hives.advice: Itchy raised welts (Urticaria) caused by histamine release. Can be triggered by allergies, stress, or temp changes.
Hives.cautions: Seek immediate help if you have trouble breathing, swelling in the throat, or feel faint (anaphylaxis).
Hives.complications: Severe allergic reaction (Anaphylaxis) and chronic hives (lasting >6 weeks).
Hives.solutions: Oral antihistamines (cetirizine, loratadine), calamine lotion, and avoidance of triggers.
Hives.doctor_advice: See an allergist if hives recur frequently or if you suspect a specific food/medicine trigger.
Hives.symptoms: Red or skin-colored raised welts, intense itching, blanching (center turns white when pressed).
Hives.prevention: Keep a food/activity diary to identify triggers and avoid known allergens.
Hives.locations: Can appear anywhere on the body, including face, limbs, and torso.
Hives.diagnosis: Clinical examination; allergy skin tests or blood tests (IgE) if chronic.
Hives.immediate_actions: Take an over-the-counter antihistamine and apply a cool compress to the itchy areas.
Hives.lifestyle: Wear loose cotton clothing and avoid hot showers which can worsen the itch.
visual_features: Borders that shift or migrate over hours
Varying sizes from millimeters to large plaques

Hyperhidrosis.advice: A condition characterized by abnormally excessive sweating that's not necessarily related to heat or exercise.
Hyperhidrosis.cautions: Can lead to social anxiety and skin maceration, which increases the risk of infections.
Hyperhidrosis.complications: Fungal infections (athlete's foot) and bacterial infections (pitted keratolysis).
Hyperhidrosis.solutions: Clinical strength antiperspirants, Botox injections, or iontophoresis.
Hyperhidrosis.doctor_advice: Consult a dermatologist if sweating disrupts your daily activities or occurs at night.
Hyperhidrosis.symptoms: Visible sweating, clammy palms, and frequent need to change clothes.
Hyperhidrosis.prevention: Use strong antiperspirants and choose moisture-wicking fabrics.
Hyperhidrosis.locations: Palms, soles of feet, armpits, and face.
Hyperhidrosis.diagnosis: Patient history; sometimes a minor starch-iodine test to identify areas of sweat.
Hyperhidrosis.immediate_actions: Use absorbent foot powders and wear leather or breathable shoes.
Hyperhidrosis.lifestyle: Wear natural fibers like cotton and practice stress-management techniques.
visual_features: Macerated (whitish, soggy) skin in affected areas

Ichthyosis Vulgaris.advice: An inherited skin disorder in which dead skin cells accumulate in thick, dry scales on the surface.
Ichthyosis Vulgaris.cautions: Condition usually worsens in cold, dry weather and improves in warm, humid weather.
Ichthyosis Vulgaris.complications: Secondary infections from skin cracks, and overheating due to impaired sweating.
Ichthyosis Vulgaris.solutions: Alpha hydroxy acids (lactic acid, glycolic acid) and retinoids to help shed skin cells.
Ichthyosis Vulgaris.doctor_advice: Consult a doctor if heavy moisturizers don't improve the scaling or if the skin looks infected.
Ichthyosis Vulgaris.symptoms: Fine, 'fish-scale' scaling, dry and thickened skin. Often associated with atopic dermatitis.
Ichthyosis Vulgaris.prevention: Genetic condition; focus on preventing flares with proper skin hydration.
Ichthyosis Vulgaris.locations: Most severe on the shins, but can affect the trunk and arms. Faces are usually spared.
Ichthyosis Vulgaris.diagnosis: Based on the appearance of scales and patient/family history.
Ichthyosis Vulgaris.immediate_actions: Use heavy, urea-based or lactic acid-based moisturizers immediately after bathing.
Ichthyosis Vulgaris.lifestyle: Take daily baths to soak and hydrate the skin; use a humidifier in the home.
visual_features: White, gray, or brown scale color

Impetigo.advice: Highly contagious bacterial infection (Staph/Strep). Common in children. Requires prescription antibiotics.
Impetigo.cautions: Keep child home from school until 24 hours after starting antibiotics and sores are covered.
Impetigo.complications: Kidney inflammation (post-strep glomerulonephritis), cellulitis, and scarring.
Impetigo.solutions: Topical antibiotic ointment (mupirocin) or oral antibiotics for widespread cases.
Impetigo.doctor_advice: Consult doctor immediately for any red sore that develops a honey-colored crust.
Impetigo.symptoms: Red sores that quickly rupture, ooze for a few days, and then form a honey-colored crust.
Impetigo.prevention: Regular hand washing, keeping skin injuries clean/covered, and not sharing personal items.
Impetigo.locations: Commonly around the nose and mouth, but can spread to limbs.
Impetigo.diagnosis: Usually diagnosed by appearance; wound culture if infection is recurrent or resistant.
Impetigo.immediate_actions: Gently wash the area with mild soap and water. Apply a bandage. See a doctor.
Impetigo.lifestyle: Wash the infected person's clothes, towels, and bedding in hot water every day.

Insect Bites.advice: Common skin reactions to bites or stings from insects like mosquitoes, fleas, or bedbugs.
Insect Bites.cautions: Watch for signs of infection (pus/heat) or systemic symptoms like fever or joint pain.
Insect Bites.complications: Cellulitis, Lyme disease (from ticks), and severe allergic reactions.
Insect Bites.solutions: Hydrocortisone cream, antihistamines, and cool compresses.
Insect Bites.doctor_advice: Consult a doctor if you develop a target-shaped rash (tick bite) or have widespread hives.
Insect Bites.symptoms: Red, itchy bumps with a central puncture mark; sometimes swelling and tenderness.
Insect Bites.prevention: Use insect repellent (DEET), wear long sleeves, and avoid areas with high insect activity.
Insect Bites.locations: Exposed skin like arms, legs, and neck.
Insect Bites.diagnosis: Based on the appearance of the lesion and history of exposure.
Insect Bites.immediate_actions: Wash the area with soap and water; avoid scratching to prevent infection.
Insect Bites.lifestyle: Check for ticks after being outdoors and use bedbug-proof mattress covers if traveling.

Intertrigo.advice: Inflammation of the skin caused by friction and moisture in skin folds.
Intertrigo.cautions: Often becomes infected with yeast (Candida) or bacteria if not kept dry.
Intertrigo.complications: Secondary yeast infection and painful skin breakdown (erosions).
Intertrigo.solutions: Keeping the area dry, using barrier ointments (zinc oxide), and antifungal creams if infected.
Intertrigo.doctor_advice: See a doctor if the rash develops an odor, becomes very painful, or shows bright red spots.
Intertrigo.symptoms: Red, raw, and itchy skin in areas where skin touches skin.
Intertrigo.prevention: Dry skin folds thoroughly after bathing and wear moisture-wicking clothing.
Intertrigo.locations: Armpits, under breasts, groin, and between stomach folds.
Intertrigo.diagnosis: Physical examination; skin scraping for yeast if necessary.
Intertrigo.immediate_actions: Apply a barrier cream and try to separate skin folds to allow air circulation.
Intertrigo.lifestyle: Manage weight if applicable and choose loose-fitting cotton underwear.
visual_features: Mirror-image erythema (redness on both sides of a fold)

Jock Itch.advice: A fungal infection (tinea cruris) that causes a red, itchy rash in the warm, moist areas of the groin.
Jock Itch.cautions: Often spreads from athlete's foot; be sure to treat both areas if both are affected.
Jock Itch.complications: Secondary bacterial infection and chronic skin discoloration.
Jock Itch.solutions: Antifungal creams, sprays, or powders used consistently for 2 weeks.
Jock Itch.doctor_advice: Consult a doctor if the rash is painful, oozing, or doesn't clear with OTC antifungals.
Jock Itch.symptoms: Red, scaly patches with a slightly raised border that may spread to the thighs but spares the scrotum.
Jock Itch.prevention: Keep the groin area dry, change underwear daily, and don't share towels.
Jock Itch.diagnosis: Visual inspection; KOH prep to confirm the presence of fungus.
Jock Itch.immediate_actions: Apply an OTC antifungal cream and switch to loose cotton boxers.
Jock Itch.lifestyle: Dry the groin thoroughly before dressing and wash gym clothes after every use.
visual_features: Central clearing as the patch expands

Keloids.advice: An overgrown scar that rises significantly above the skin and is much larger than the original wound.
Keloids.cautions: Surgical removal alone often results in the keloid returning even larger. Not cancerous.
Keloids.complications: Itching, pain, and restricted movement if near a joint.
Keloids.solutions: Steroid injections to flatten the scar, silicone sheets, and laser treatments.
Keloids.doctor_advice: See a dermatologist for treatment options if the scar is itchy or bothersome.
Keloids.symptoms: A thick, raised, firm, and shiny scar that expands beyond the original injury.
Keloids.prevention: Avoid unnecessary piercings or surgery if you have a known history of keloid formation.
Keloids.diagnosis: Physical examination based on the characteristic appearance of the scar.
Keloids.immediate_actions: Apply silicone gel or sheets early in the healing process of a wound.
Keloids.lifestyle: Wear loose clothing to avoid irritation and protect the scar from sun exposure which can darken it.
visual_features: Expansion beyond borders of initial injury

Keratoacanthoma.advice: A rapid-growing skin tumor that resembles squamous cell carcinoma. It often resolves on its own but excision is recommended.
Keratoacanthoma.cautions: Because it looks identical to SCC, all such lesions should be treated by a professional.
Keratoacanthoma.complications: Local tissue destruction due to rapid growth or uncertainty in diagnosis versus SCC.
Keratoacanthoma.solutions: Surgical excision is the standard. Other options include cryosurgery or intralesional injections.
Keratoacanthoma.doctor_advice: Seek immediate medical attention for any fast-growing skin nodule with a central plug.
Keratoacanthoma.symptoms: A fast-growing, dome-shaped nodule with a central keratinous horn. Usually painless.
Keratoacanthoma.prevention: Limit sun exposure and use protective measures against UV radiation.
Keratoacanthoma.locations: Face, neck, arms, and back of hands.
Keratoacanthoma.diagnosis: Excisional biopsy is necessary to differentiate from invasive SCC.
Keratoacanthoma.immediate_actions: Schedule an urgent dermatology appointment due to the rapid growth rate.
Keratoacanthoma.lifestyle: Strict sun protection to prevent future skin cancers.

Keratosis Pilaris.advice: A common, harmless skin condition (often called 'chicken skin') caused by keratin buildup in hair follicles.
Keratosis Pilaris.cautions: Picking at the bumps can lead to scarring or infection. It tends to improve with age.
Keratosis Pilaris.complications: Minor cosmetic concern and occasional itching.
Keratosis Pilaris.solutions: Moisturizers containing urea, salicylic acid, or lactic acid to help exfoliate and soften.
Keratosis Pilaris.doctor_advice: See a doctor for persistent itching or if the skin looks very red and inflamed.
Keratosis Pilaris.symptoms: Small, painless bumps that feel like sandpaper; sometimes surrounded by mild redness.
Keratosis Pilaris.prevention: Maintain skin moisture; there is no permanent cure as it is often genetic.
Keratosis Pilaris.locations: Backs of upper arms, thighs, and buttocks.
Keratosis Pilaris.diagnosis: Based on the characteristic 'sandpaper' texture and location of the bumps.
Keratosis Pilaris.immediate_actions: Apply a thick, exfoliating moisturizer twice daily.
Keratosis Pilaris.lifestyle: Avoid harsh soaps and take short, lukewarm showers to prevent drying the skin further.

Lamellar Ichthyosis.advice: A rare but severe genetic condition where babies are born with a 'collodion' membrane that sheds into large scales.
Lamellar Ichthyosis.cautions: Requires lifelong specialized skin care. Patients are prone to infections and dehydration.
Lamellar Ichthyosis.complications: Ectropion (eyelids turning out), alopecia (hair loss), and impaired thermoregulation.
Lamellar Ichthyosis.solutions: High doses of moisturizers and oral retinoids (acitretin) under specialist supervision.
Lamellar Ichthyosis.doctor_advice: Lifelong monitoring by a dermatologist specializing in genetic skin disorders.
Lamellar Ichthyosis.symptoms: Large, dark, plate-like scales covering most of the body. Skin feels very tight.
Lamellar Ichthyosis.prevention: Inherited condition; genetic counseling is recommended for families.
Lamellar Ichthyosis.locations: Generalized involvement covering the entire body surface.
Lamellar Ichthyosis.diagnosis: Clinical features confirmed by skin biopsy and genetic testing.
Lamellar Ichthyosis.immediate_actions: Apply prescribed emollient therapy frequently to prevent skin cracking.
Lamellar Ichthyosis.lifestyle: Keep the environment humid and avoid overheating as sweating is limited.

Lichen Planus.advice: An inflammatory condition that can affect skin, hair, nails, and mucous membranes (mouth).
Lichen Planus.cautions: May be associated with Hepatitis C. Lesions in the mouth can occasionally become cancerous.
Lichen Planus.complications: Significant scarring (especially on the scalp/nails) and persistent oral ulcers.
Lichen Planus.solutions: Topical and oral steroids, phototherapy, or immunosuppressive drugs.
Lichen Planus.doctor_advice: See a doctor for itchy, flat-topped purple bumps or white lacy patches in the mouth.
Lichen Planus.symptoms: The 6 P's: Planar (flat-topped), Purple, Polygonal, Pruritic (itchy), Papules, and Plaques.
Lichen Planus.prevention: No known prevention; manage stress and avoid skin trauma.
Lichen Planus.locations: Wrists, ankles, lower back, and inside the mouth.
Lichen Planus.diagnosis: Visual inspection of lesions and 'Wickham striae'; confirmed by skin biopsy.
Lichen Planus.immediate_actions: Use cool compresses to manage itching and avoid scratching the bumps.
Lichen Planus.lifestyle: Maintain good oral hygiene; avoid spicy or acidic foods if mouth is involved.

Lichen Simplex Chronicus.advice: A skin condition characterized by chronic itching and scratching, which leads to thick, leathery (lichenified) skin.
Lichen Simplex Chronicus.cautions: Breaking the 'itch-scratch cycle' is the most critical part of treatment.
Lichen Simplex Chronicus.complications: Secondary bacterial infection and permanent skin changes.
Lichen Simplex Chronicus.solutions: High-potency topical steroids, covering the area to prevent scratching, and anti-itch medications.
Lichen Simplex Chronicus.doctor_advice: Consult a dermatologist if you can't stop scratching certain areas of skin.
Lichen Simplex Chronicus.symptoms: A thick, leathery patch of skin that is intensely itchy, especially at night.
Lichen Simplex Chronicus.prevention: Avoid scratching minor skin irritations to prevent the cycle from starting.
Lichen Simplex Chronicus.locations: Nape of neck, ankles, wrists, and groin area.
Lichen Simplex Chronicus.diagnosis: Physical exam showing accentuated skin lines (lichenification).
Lichen Simplex Chronicus.immediate_actions: Apply a thick moisturizer and cover the area with a bandage to prevent scratching.
Lichen Simplex Chronicus.lifestyle: Keep fingernails trimmed short and identify stress factors that may increase itching.

Lipomas.advice: Benign (non-cancerous) fatty tumors that grow slowly just under the skin.
Lipomas.cautions: Usually harmless; they only need removal if they become painful or grow very large.
Lipomas.complications: Compression of nearby nerves (causing pain) and cosmetic concern.
Lipomas.solutions: Monitoring, surgical excision, or liposuction for removal.
Lipomas.doctor_advice: See a doctor for any new or growing lump to confirm it is a lipoma and not something else.
Lipomas.symptoms: A soft, doughy lump that moves easily with slight finger pressure. Painless unless pushing on a nerve.
Lipomas.prevention: No known prevention; they are a common type of soft tissue tumor.
Lipomas.diagnosis: Physical examination; ultrasound or biopsy if the lump feels firm or deep.
Lipomas.immediate_actions: Avoid trying to 'massage away' or squeeze the lump.
Lipomas.lifestyle: Monitor the lump for changes in size or consistency.

Livedo Reticularis.advice: A condition causing a lacy, net-like pattern of reddish-blue discoloration on the skin.
Livedo Reticularis.cautions: Often harmless when caused by cold (physiologic), but can indicate underlying vascular issues.
Livedo Reticularis.complications: Blood clots (thrombosis) or skin ulcers if caused by an underlying autoimmune disease.
Livedo Reticularis.solutions: Rewarming the skin; treating the underlying condition if the pattern is persistent.
Livedo Reticularis.doctor_advice: See a doctor if the pattern is permanent, painful, or associated with skin sores.
Livedo Reticularis.symptoms: Net-like or mottled appearance of the skin, most visible when cold.
Livedo Reticularis.prevention: Keep the body warm and avoid exposure to cold environments.
Livedo Reticularis.diagnosis: Visual examination; blood tests for autoimmune disorders (like Lupus) if persistent.
Livedo Reticularis.immediate_actions: Warm up the body and see if the pattern disappears.
Livedo Reticularis.lifestyle: Wear warm clothing and avoid smoking, which can worsen circulation.

Lupus.advice: A systemic autoimmune disease. Skin-only (discoid) or systemic (SLE) forms require expert medical management.
Lupus.cautions: Extreme sun sensitivity. UV exposure can flare not just the skin but also internal organ disease.
Lupus.complications: Scarring alopecia, permanent skin discoloration, and internal organ damage (kidneys, heart).
Lupus.solutions: Anti-malarials (hydroxychloroquine), topical steroids, and systemic immunosuppressants.
Lupus.doctor_advice: Seek medical review for any butterfly-shaped rash on the face or coin-shaped scarring sores.
Lupus.symptoms: Butterfly rash across cheeks, sun-sensitive rashes, joint pain, and fatigue.
Lupus.prevention: Strict UV avoidance: high-SPF sunscreen, UPF clothing, and avoiding mid-day sun.
Lupus.locations: Face (malar area), scalp, ears, and sun-exposed chest/arms.
Lupus.diagnosis: Skin biopsy and detailed blood work (ANA, anti-dsDNA, etc.).
Lupus.immediate_actions: Wear a wide-brimmed hat and avoid all direct sun exposure until evaluated by a doctor.
Lupus.lifestyle: Quit smoking (worsens lupus) and maintain regular follow-ups with rheumatology.
visual_features: Heliotrope rash (on eyes in some overlaps)

Melanoma.advice: The most dangerous form of skin cancer. Early detection and surgical removal are key to survival.
Melanoma.cautions: Follow the ABCDE rule. Any change in an existing mole or a new suspicious spot requires immediate biopsy.
Melanoma.complications: Metastasis to internal organs (lungs, liver, brain) and lymph nodes. Can be fatal.
Melanoma.solutions: Wide surgical excision, lymph node mapping, and potentially immunotherapy or targeted therapy.
Melanoma.doctor_advice: Urgent consultation is mandatory for any lesion meeting the ABCDE criteria.
Melanoma.symptoms: Growth of an existing mole, changing shape/color, itchiness, or bleeding.
Melanoma.prevention: Regular skin self-exams, professional checks, and avoidance of excessive UV light/tanning.
Melanoma.locations: Can occur anywhere, including areas not exposed to the sun (soles, nails).
Melanoma.diagnosis: Full excisional biopsy; staging via imaging or sentinel lymph node biopsy if invasive.
Melanoma.immediate_actions: Do not wait. Schedule an appointment with a dermatologist or specialist today.
Melanoma.lifestyle: Lifelong sun protection and regular professional skin monitoring.
visual_features: Multiple colors (tan, brown, black, red, blue, or white)
Evolution (changes in size, shape, or color over time)

Melasma.advice: A common skin condition that causes brown or gray-brown patches, usually on the face. Often called the 'mask of pregnancy.'
Melasma.cautions: Sun exposure is the primary trigger. Even a small amount of sun can cause melasma to return after it has faded.
Melasma.complications: Significant psychological distress and social anxiety; no physical health risks.
Melasma.solutions: Sun protection is the most important treatment. Topical creams (hydroquinone, retinoids, azelaic acid) and chemical peels.
Melasma.doctor_advice: Consult a dermatologist for a customized treatment plan, especially if it is pregnancy-related.
Melasma.symptoms: Symmetrical, dark-colored patches on the face, especially the cheeks, bridge of the nose, forehead, and upper lip.
Melasma.prevention: Strict sun protection: broad-spectrum SPF 30+ sunscreen daily and wearing wide-brimmed hats.
Melasma.locations: Cheeks, upper lip, chin, and forehead.
Melasma.diagnosis: Visual examination; Wood's lamp examination help determine the depth of pigmentation.
Melasma.immediate_actions: Apply a high-quality physical sunblock immediately and avoid any harsh facial scrubs.
Melasma.lifestyle: Use gentle, fragrance-free skincare products. Avoid hormonal triggers if possible.
visual_features: Color ranging from light brown to muddy gray

Milia.advice: Small, white, firm bumps that often appear on the face. They are tiny cysts filled with keratin.
Milia.cautions: Do not try to squeeze or pop them like pimples; they are deep and have no opening to the surface.
Milia.complications: Inflammation or scarring if aggressively squeezed at home.
Milia.solutions: Often resolve on their own. Professional extraction by a dermatologist or use of topical retinoids.
Milia.doctor_advice: Consult a professional if they are cosmetically bothersome or don't resolve on their own.
Milia.symptoms: Small (1-2mm), pearly white or yellowish bumps on the skin. Usually not itchy or painful.
Milia.prevention: Regular exfoliation and using light, non-comedogenic facial moisturizers.
Milia.locations: Common around the eyes, cheeks, and nose.
Milia.diagnosis: Visual inspection by a healthcare provider.
Milia.immediate_actions: Stop using heavy, oil-based facial creams that may be clogging pores.
Milia.lifestyle: Maintain a consistent, gentle skincare routine and avoid sun damage.

Molluscum Contagiosum.advice: This is a viral infection that is usually harmless and resolves on its own over time.
Molluscum Contagiosum.cautions: The virus is highly contagious. Avoid sharing towels, razors, or athletic equipment.
Molluscum Contagiosum.complications: Secondary bacterial infection from scratching, or conjunctivitis if near the eyes.
Molluscum Contagiosum.solutions: Most resolve without treatment. Options include cryotherapy, curettage, or topical therapies.
Molluscum Contagiosum.doctor_advice: See a doctor if the bumps are widespread, painful, or in sensitive areas.
Molluscum Contagiosum.symptoms: Small, firm, painless bumps that may become itchy or red.
Molluscum Contagiosum.prevention: Avoid direct skin contact with infected persons and do not share personal items.
Molluscum Contagiosum.locations: Anywhere on the body; face, trunk, and extremities are common in children.
Molluscum Contagiosum.diagnosis: Visual inspection of the characteristic bumps.
Molluscum Contagiosum.immediate_actions: Do not pick or scratch the bumps to prevent spreading them to other body parts.
Molluscum Contagiosum.lifestyle: Keep the bumps covered with clothing or a bandage to prevent transmission.

Moles (Nevi).advice: Common skin growths (melanocytic nevi) that are usually harmless. Most people have between 10 and 40 moles.
Moles (Nevi).cautions: Monitor moles for the ABCDEs: Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Color changes, Diameter >6mm, and Evolution.
Moles (Nevi).complications: Potential for development into melanoma (skin cancer), especially with changing moles.
Moles (Nevi).solutions: Monitoring and surgical excision if there are signs of atypical change (dysplastic nevi).
Moles (Nevi).doctor_advice: Consult a dermatologist for any mole that starts to bleed, itch, or change rapidly.
Moles (Nevi).symptoms: A small, brown or tan spot on the skin. Can be flat or raised.
Moles (Nevi).prevention: Practice sun safety: use sunscreen, wear protective clothing, and avoid tanning beds.
Moles (Nevi).locations: Anywhere on the body; often on sun-exposed areas.
Moles (Nevi).diagnosis: Visual inspection by a professional; dermoscopy and biopsy if suspicious.
Moles (Nevi).immediate_actions: Take a photo of the mole next to a ruler to track its size over time.
Moles (Nevi).lifestyle: Perform monthly skin self-exams to check for new or changing spots.

Nummular Dermatitis.advice: A type of eczema characterized by coin-shaped, itchy, and sometimes oozing patches of skin.
Nummular Dermatitis.cautions: Can be triggered by dry skin, minor injuries, or sensitivity to certain metals (like nickel).
Nummular Dermatitis.complications: Secondary bacterial infection (Staph) and severe itching leading to skin breakdown.
Nummular Dermatitis.solutions: High-potency topical steroids, thick moisturizers, and oral antihistamines.
Nummular Dermatitis.doctor_advice: See a dermatologist for persistent coin-shaped rashes that don't respond to moisturizing.
Nummular Dermatitis.symptoms: Itchy, round, red patches that may be scaly or have small blisters.
Nummular Dermatitis.prevention: Prevent skin dryness, use gentle cleansers, and avoid skin trauma.
Nummular Dermatitis.locations: Most common on the arms and legs.
Nummular Dermatitis.diagnosis: Visual examination; skin scraping (KOH) to rule out ringworm if the center is clear.
Nummular Dermatitis.immediate_actions: Apply a thick, unscented moisturizer to the area multiple times a day.
Nummular Dermatitis.lifestyle: Avoid long, hot showers and wear soft, natural fabrics like cotton.

Paronychia.advice: An infection of the skin around a fingernail or toenail. Can be acute (bacterial) or chronic (yeast).
Paronychia.cautions: If the area is very swollen and painful, it may require drainage by a doctor.
Paronychia.complications: Abscess formation and potential damage to the nail plate.
Paronychia.solutions: Warm water soaks, topical or oral antibiotics (for acute), and antifungals (for chronic).
Paronychia.doctor_advice: Consult a doctor if the infection spreads or if there is a visible collection of pus.
Paronychia.symptoms: Redness, swelling, and tenderness in the skin around the nail.
Paronychia.prevention: Avoid biting nails, picking at cuticles, and keeping hands submerged in water for too long.
Paronychia.diagnosis: Diagnosed by clinical appearance; culture of pus to identify the specific bug.
Paronychia.immediate_actions: Soak the finger in warm water for 15 minutes three times a day.
Paronychia.lifestyle: Wear gloves for wet work and use moisturizing hand cream to prevent skin cracks.
visual_features: Distortion of the nail in chronic cases

Pediculosis.advice: An infestation of lice (head, body, or pubic) that feed on human blood and cause intense itching.
Pediculosis.cautions: Highly contagious through head-to-head contact or sharing personal items like hats or combs.
Pediculosis.complications: Secondary bacterial infection from intense scratching and social distress.
Pediculosis.solutions: Topical treatments (permethrin), fine-tooth combing to remove nits, and washing bedding in hot water.
Pediculosis.doctor_advice: Consult a doctor if OTC treatments fail or if the child is very young.
Pediculosis.symptoms: Intense itching, visible lice, and tiny white 'nits' (eggs) glued to hair shafts.
Pediculosis.prevention: Avoid sharing brushes, hats, or earphones; regular screening in school settings.
Pediculosis.locations: Scalp (head lice) or body and pubic areas.
Pediculosis.diagnosis: Visual detection of live lice or nits in the hair or on clothing.
Pediculosis.immediate_actions: Begin treatment with a lice-killing shampoo and wash all recently used linens in hot water.
Pediculosis.lifestyle: Inform school or daycare and check all household members for infestation.
visual_features: Small, white, oval nits near the scalp

Pemphigus Vulgaris.advice: A life-threatening autoimmune disease causing severe blistering of the skin and mucous membranes (mouth).
Pemphigus Vulgaris.cautions: Requires immediate hospitalization in severe cases. Fatal if left untreated due to infection and dehydration.
Pemphigus Vulgaris.complications: Sepsis, severe electrolyte imbalance, and widespread painful erosions.
Pemphigus Vulgaris.solutions: High-dose corticosteroids and biologics (rituximab) are the current standard of care.
Pemphigus Vulgaris.doctor_advice: Seek immediate emergency care for painful blisters in the mouth that spread to the skin.
Pemphigus Vulgaris.symptoms: Extremely painful sores in the mouth followed by fragile, flaccid blisters on the skin.
Pemphigus Vulgaris.prevention: Not preventable; caused by the body's immune system attacking its own skin-binding proteins.
Pemphigus Vulgaris.locations: Mouth, scalp, face, and torso. Can affect all mucous membranes.
Pemphigus Vulgaris.diagnosis: Nikolsky sign (positive), skin biopsy, and immunofluorescence blood tests.
Pemphigus Vulgaris.immediate_actions: Go to an emergency department or specialist urgently.
Pemphigus Vulgaris.lifestyle: Requires lifelong specialist monitoring and often long-term immunosuppression.
visual_features: Positive Nikolsky sign (skin shears with friction)

Perioral Dermatitis.advice: An inflammatory skin rash around the mouth, often consisting of tiny red bumps and scaling.
Perioral Dermatitis.cautions: Triggered or worsened by topical steroid use; avoid applying hydrocortisone to the face.
Perioral Dermatitis.complications: Significant facial redness and social distress; potential scarring from picking.
Perioral Dermatitis.solutions: Gentle skincare, oral or topical antibiotics (metronidazole, tetracycline), and stopping steroids.
Perioral Dermatitis.doctor_advice: Consult a dermatologist if you have a persistent rash around the mouth or eyes.
Perioral Dermatitis.symptoms: Small red papules, sometimes with tiny pustules, and a clearing right around the lip border.
Perioral Dermatitis.prevention: Avoid heavy facial creams and topical steroids on the face.
Perioral Dermatitis.locations: Around the mouth, nose, and eyes (periocular).
Perioral Dermatitis.diagnosis: Clinical appearance; distinguishing it from acne or rosacea is key.
Perioral Dermatitis.immediate_actions: Stop using all facial products except a very gentle cleanser and water.
Perioral Dermatitis.lifestyle: Identify if toothpaste with fluoride or heavy night creams are triggers.
visual_features: Spare zone (clear skin) immediately around the lips

Photoaging.advice: Premature aging of the skin caused by repeated exposure to ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the sun.
Photoaging.cautions: Increases the risk of all types of skin cancer, including life-threatening melanoma.
Photoaging.complications: Wrinkles, leathery skin, and development of precancerous actinic keratoses.
Photoaging.solutions: Sun protection, topical retinoids (tretinoin), and aesthetic procedures like lasers or chemical peels.
Photoaging.doctor_advice: See a dermatologist for periodic skin checks if you have a history of heavy sun exposure.
Photoaging.symptoms: Deep wrinkles, dark 'liver' spots, and a yellow or leathery texture to the skin.
Photoaging.prevention: Strict sun protection: SPF 30+, hats, and avoiding peak sun hours.
Photoaging.locations: Face, neck, backs of hands, and chest.
Photoaging.diagnosis: Clinical examination based on visual signs of sun damage.
Photoaging.immediate_actions: Start a daily broad-spectrum sunscreen habit immediately.
Photoaging.lifestyle: Adopt a skincare routine including antioxidants (Vitamin C) and sun-protective clothing.

Pityriasis Rosea.advice: A common, harmless inflammatory skin rash that starts with a large 'herald patch' followed by many smaller spots.
Pityriasis Rosea.cautions: Often mistaken for ringworm, but it does not respond to antifungal creams. It is self-limiting.
Pityriasis Rosea.complications: Occasional intense itching and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.
Pityriasis Rosea.solutions: Reassurance (it goes away on its own in 6-12 weeks), topical steroids for itch, and sun exposure.
Pityriasis Rosea.doctor_advice: See a doctor if the rash lasts longer than 3 months or if it is very itchy.
Pityriasis Rosea.symptoms: One large oval scaly patch (herald patch) followed by multiple smaller scaly pink oval spots.
Pityriasis Rosea.prevention: No known prevention; it is thought to be triggered by a common virus (HHV-6 or HHV-7).
Pityriasis Rosea.locations: Chest, back (Christmas tree pattern), and abdomen.
Pityriasis Rosea.diagnosis: Diagnosed by the unique 'Christmas tree' distribution on the trunk.
Pityriasis Rosea.immediate_actions: Don't panic; it is not contagious and will resolve without treatment.
Pityriasis Rosea.lifestyle: Use lukewarm baths and stay cool to avoid irritating the itch.
visual_features: Smaller secondary papules in 'Christmas tree' distribution

Poison Ivy.advice: An allergic contact dermatitis (Rhus dermatitis) caused by contact with urushiol oil from poison ivy, oak, or sumac.
Poison Ivy.cautions: Urushiol oil can stay on surfaces or pet fur for months. Avoid smoke from burning poison ivy.
Poison Ivy.complications: Secondary bacterial infection (from scratching) and severe systemic reactions.
Poison Ivy.solutions: Washing the oil off immediately, topical steroids, and oral steroids for severe cases.
Poison Ivy.doctor_advice: See a doctor if the rash is on your face/eyes or covers more than 25% of your body.
Poison Ivy.symptoms: Intense itching, redness, swelling, and blisters that often appear in linear (straight line) patterns.
