Poison Ivy.prevention: Learn to identify the plants ('leaves of three, let them be') and wear protective clothing.
Poison Ivy.locations: Any area that contacted the plant oil.
Poison Ivy.diagnosis: Clinical examination based on the linear arrangement of blisters and history of exposure.
Poison Ivy.immediate_actions: Wash the affected skin and any clothing/tools with soap and water immediately.
Poison Ivy.lifestyle: Use barrier creams (Tecnu) before going into high-risk areas.

Polymorphic Light Eruption.advice: A common form of 'sun poisoning' or sensitivity, causing an itchy rash after exposure to sunlight.
Polymorphic Light Eruption.cautions: Usually occurs in early spring or summer when skin is first exposed to intense sun.
Polymorphic Light Eruption.complications: Discomfort and social embarrassment; potential for secondary infection from scratching.
Polymorphic Light Eruption.solutions: Sun protection, gradually increasing sun exposure (hardening), and topical steroids.
Polymorphic Light Eruption.doctor_advice: Consult a dermatologist for testing (phototesting) to confirm the diagnosis.
Polymorphic Light Eruption.symptoms: Itchy, red bumps or plaques that appear within hours or days of sun exposure.
Polymorphic Light Eruption.prevention: Wears protective clothing and use high-SPF, broad-spectrum sunscreen.
Polymorphic Light Eruption.locations: Sun-exposed areas like the chest, neck, and arms.
Polymorphic Light Eruption.diagnosis: Patient history and clinical appearance; phototesting if diagnosis is in doubt.
Polymorphic Light Eruption.immediate_actions: Stay out of the sun and apply a cool compress to the rash.
Polymorphic Light Eruption.lifestyle: Plan outdoor activities for early morning or late evening when UV levels are lower.
visual_features: Polymorphic (variable) appearance: papules, plaques, or blisters
Sparing of shaded areas (like under the chin)

Psoriasis.advice: A chronic autoimmune condition that speeds up the growth cycle of skin cells, leading to thick, scaly patches.
Psoriasis.cautions: Can overlap with psoriatic arthritis. Avoid triggers like stress, smoking, and infections.
Psoriasis.complications: Psoriatic arthritis (joint damage), increased risk of cardiovascular disease, and metabolic syndrome.
Psoriasis.solutions: Topical steroids, vitamin D analogues, phototherapy, and systemic biologics.
Psoriasis.doctor_advice: See a doctor if scales are widespread or if you have joint stiffness/pain.
Psoriasis.symptoms: Red patches of skin covered with thick, silvery scales; dry, cracked skin; and itching or burning.
Psoriasis.prevention: Maintain a healthy lifestyle and avoid known triggers to reduce flare frequency.
Psoriasis.locations: Elbows, knees, scalp, and lower back.
Psoriasis.diagnosis: Physical examination; skin biopsy helps differentiate from other scaly conditions.
Psoriasis.immediate_actions: Apply a thick moisturizer to soften scales and avoid picking at them.
Psoriasis.lifestyle: Manage stress, maintain a healthy weight, and use sunlight in moderation (phototherapy).
visual_features: Auspitz sign (pinpoint bleeding when scales are removed)

Psoriatic Arthritis.advice: An inflammatory arthritis associated with psoriasis. Can cause permanent joint damage if not treated early.
Psoriatic Arthritis.cautions: Always report joint pain, stiffness, or swelling to your dermatologist if you have psoriasis.
Psoriatic Arthritis.complications: Joint deformity, loss of function, and chronic pain.
Psoriatic Arthritis.solutions: NSAIDs for pain, and DMARDs or biologics to prevent joint destruction.
Psoriatic Arthritis.doctor_advice: Requires specialized care from a rheumatologist alongside a dermatologist.
Psoriatic Arthritis.symptoms: Swollen 'sausage-like' fingers or toes (dactylitis), morning stiffness, and back pain.
Psoriatic Arthritis.prevention: Early detection and aggressive treatment of underlying psoriasis can reduce risk.
Psoriatic Arthritis.locations: Fingere joints, toes, wrists, and the spine (sacroiliitis).
Psoriatic Arthritis.diagnosis: Clinical history, imaging (X-rays/MRI), and blood tests to rule out rheumatoid arthritis.
Psoriatic Arthritis.immediate_actions: Schedule a rheumatology consultation if you have joint pain and skin psoriasis.
Psoriatic Arthritis.lifestyle: Regular low-impact exercise and weight management to reduce joint stress.
visual_features: Swelling of an entire digit (sausage digit)

Purpura.advice: Purple-colored spots (bruising) on the skin caused by blood vessels leaking or bursting under the surface.
Purpura.cautions: Large areas of purpura (ecchymosis) or pinpoint spots (petechiae) can indicate serious blood or clotting disorders.
Purpura.complications: Internal bleeding or organ damage if part of a systemic disease (like vasculitis).
Purpura.solutions: Treating the underlying cause; sometimes requires steroids or immunosuppressants.
Purpura.doctor_advice: Seek immediate medical care for any purple spots that do not turn white when pressed (non-blanching).
Purpura.symptoms: Purple, red, or brownish spots that do not fade with pressure. Can be flat or raised.
Purpura.prevention: No specific prevention; manage blood pressure and avoid medications that cause bleeding if possible.
Purpura.locations: Most common on the legs and arms.
Purpura.diagnosis: Based on the non-blanching characteristic; blood tests and potential skin biopsy.
Purpura.immediate_actions: Press a clear glass against the spot to see if it pales; if it doesn't, see a doctor promptly.
Purpura.lifestyle: Be careful to avoid minor skin trauma if you have fragile blood vessels (actinic purpura).

Pyogenic Granuloma.advice: A common, benign skin growth that is small, red, and often oozes or bleeds easily.
Pyogenic Granuloma.cautions: Despite the name, it is not infectious (pyogenic) or a true granuloma; it is a vascular growth.
Pyogenic Granuloma.complications: Frequent heavy bleeding from minor trauma and recurrence if not completely removed.
Pyogenic Granuloma.solutions: Surgical excision, curettage, or laser treatment to remove the lesion completely.
Pyogenic Granuloma.doctor_advice: Consult a dermatologist for a rapidly growing, bleeding red bump to rule out other conditions.
Pyogenic Granuloma.symptoms: A fast-growing red, purple, or brown-black bump that bleeds with very little pressure.
Pyogenic Granuloma.prevention: No known prevention; often triggered by minor skin injuries or hormonal changes (pregnancy).
Pyogenic Granuloma.diagnosis: Clinical appearance and history of rapid growth; confirmed by biopsy after removal.
Pyogenic Granuloma.immediate_actions: Apply firm pressure to stop any bleeding and see a doctor for removal.
Pyogenic Granuloma.lifestyle: Avoid picking at the lesion and keep it covered with a bandage until it can be treated.
visual_features: Often surrounded by a 'collar' of scale

Rashes.advice: A broad term for any inflammatory skin change that alters the color, appearance, or texture of the skin.
Rashes.cautions: Rashes can be caused by allergies, infections, heat, or underlying systemic diseases. Seek ER care for a high fever + rash.
Rashes.complications: Secondary bacterial infection (from scratching) and skin thickening or scarring.
Rashes.solutions: Treatment depends on the cause; common options include moisturizers, topical steroids, and antihistamines.
Rashes.doctor_advice: Consult a doctor if the rash is painful, widespread, or fails to improve within a week.
Rashes.symptoms: Redness, bumps, scales, or blisters; can be localized or generalized.
Rashes.prevention: Avoid known allergens, maintain skin hydration, and use gentle, fragrance-free products.
Rashes.locations: Can occur on any part of the body.
Rashes.diagnosis: Based on the rash's appearance, location, and associated symptoms.
Rashes.immediate_actions: Wash the area gently and apply a cool, damp cloth if it is itchy or burning.
Rashes.lifestyle: Maintain a symptom log to help identify triggers like specific soaps or foods.
visual_features: Various morphologies: papules, macules, or vesicles

Raynaud's Phenomenon.advice: A condition in which smaller arteries that supply blood to your skin narrow, limiting blood circulation to affected areas.
Raynaud's Phenomenon.cautions: Can be a standalone condition (primary) or a sign of an underlying autoimmune disease like Lupus or Scleroderma (secondary).
Raynaud's Phenomenon.complications: Skin ulcers or even gangrene (tissue death) if blood flow is severely restricted for long periods.
Raynaud's Phenomenon.solutions: Keeping the body warm, managing stress, and medications like calcium channel blockers to open blood vessels.
Raynaud's Phenomenon.doctor_advice: Consult a doctor if your fingers turn white/blue when cold, especially if ulcers develop.
Raynaud's Phenomenon.symptoms: Fingers or toes turning white, then blue, then red. Numbness or a 'pins and needles' sensation.
Raynaud's Phenomenon.prevention: Dress warmly in cold weather, wear gloves when handling cold items, and avoid smoking.
Raynaud's Phenomenon.locations: Fingers and toes; occasionally the nose and ears.
Raynaud's Phenomenon.diagnosis: Based on patient history and cold-stimulation tests; blood work for secondary causes.
Raynaud's Phenomenon.immediate_actions: Move to a warmer environment and gently wiggle fingers/toes to encourage blood flow.
Raynaud's Phenomenon.lifestyle: Avoid sudden temperature changes and use hand warmers during outdoor activities.
visual_features: Blue (cyanosis) due to lack of oxygen

Ringworm.advice: A common fungal infection that responds well to antifungal treatments. It is contagious!
Ringworm.cautions: Keep the area clean and dry. Avoid sharing personal items with others.
Ringworm.complications: Secondary bacterial infection or permanent hair loss in scalp cases (tinea capitis).
Ringworm.solutions: Topical antifungal creams (clotrimazole, terbinafine). Oral meds for severe cases.
Ringworm.doctor_advice: Consult a doctor if the rash does not improve after 2 weeks of over-the-counter treatment.
Ringworm.symptoms: Ring-shaped, red, itchy rash with clearer skin in the center.
Ringworm.prevention: Keep skin dry, wear shoes in public showers, and avoid contact with infected animals.
Ringworm.locations: Body (tinea corporis), scalp, groin (jock itch), or feet (athlete's foot).
Ringworm.diagnosis: Clinical examination or KOH prep skin scraping.
Ringworm.immediate_actions: Apply an OTC antifungal cream. Wash hands thoroughly after touching the area.
Ringworm.lifestyle: Wear loose, breathable clothing and avoid tight synthetic fabrics.
visual_features: Central clearing (skin looks healthier in the middle)

Rosacea.advice: A chronic condition that primarily affects the face. Identifying and avoiding triggers is key.
Rosacea.cautions: Avoid harsh skincare products and spicy foods or alcohol if they trigger flushing.
Rosacea.complications: Ocular rosacea (eye damage) or thickened skin on the nose (rhinophyma).
Rosacea.solutions: Gentle skin care, sun protection, and prescription topical or oral treatments.
Rosacea.doctor_advice: See a dermatologist for persistent redness or if your eyes feel gritty or irritated.
Rosacea.symptoms: Persistent facial redness, visible blood vessels, and acne-like bumps.
Rosacea.prevention: Sun protection and identifying individual triggers (heat, stress, certain foods).
Rosacea.locations: Central face: cheeks, nose, forehead, and chin.
Rosacea.diagnosis: Clinical examination based on symptoms and skin appearance.
Rosacea.immediate_actions: Use a gentle, non-soap cleanser and apply broad-spectrum sunscreen.
Rosacea.lifestyle: Keep a diary to track triggers and use soothing, cool compresses.
visual_features: Papules and pustules on the face

Scabies.advice: A highly contagious infestation caused by mites. Entire households usually require treatment.
Scabies.cautions: Intense itching often worsens at night. It can spread quickly in group settings.
Scabies.complications: Secondary bacterial infections (impetigo) from scratching, which can lead to kidney issues.
Scabies.solutions: Prescription scabicide creams (permethrin) or oral medication (ivermectin).
Scabies.doctor_advice: Seek medical diagnosis immediately if you suspect scabies to prevent a wider outbreak.
Scabies.symptoms: Severe itching, thin burrow tracks on the skin, and a pimple-like rash.
Scabies.prevention: Avoid direct skin contact with infected persons and wash bedding in hot water.
Scabies.locations: Finger webs, wrists, elbows, armpits, waistline, and genitalia.
Scabies.diagnosis: Skin scraping to look for mites, eggs, or fecal matter under a microscope.
Scabies.immediate_actions: Wash all recently used clothing and bedding at 60°C. Notify close contacts.
Scabies.lifestyle: Apply treatment to the entire body from the neck down and leave on for 8-14 hours.

Scales.advice: Thin, dry flakes of skin that represent lost outer layers of the epidermis.
Scales.cautions: Scales are a symptom of many conditions, including psoriasis, eczema, and fungal infections.
Scales.complications: Can lead to skin cracks (fissures) and secondary infections if skin is not protected.
Scales.solutions: Thick moisturizers, exfoliating creams (containing urea or lactic acid), and treating the underlying cause.
Scales.doctor_advice: See a doctor if scaling is widespread, associated with intense redness, or affects your sleep.
Scales.symptoms: Visible white or gray flakes on the skin; skin may feel rough or dry.
Scales.prevention: Keep skin hydrated and avoid harsh detergents or extremely hot showers.
Scales.locations: Can occur anywhere, but common on legs, elbows, and scalp.
Scales.diagnosis: Visual examination; biopsy or skin scraping if the cause is unclear.
Scales.immediate_actions: Apply a thick emollient immediately after a 5-minute lukewarm bath.
Scales.lifestyle: Use a humidifier in dry indoor environments to help maintain skin moisture.

Scars.advice: The body's natural way of healing and replacing lost or damaged skin. Most scars are flat and pale.
Scars.cautions: Sunkissed (tanned) scars may permanently darken; keep healing scars protected from the sun.
Scars.complications: Hypertrophic scars (raised), keloids, or atrophic (pitted) scars like those from acne.
Scars.solutions: Silicone gels/sheets, laser therapy, and chemical peels to improve appearance.
Scars.doctor_advice: Consult a doctor if a scar becomes very thick, itchy, or restricts your movement.
Scars.symptoms: Changes in skin texture, color, and sometimes a lack of hair growth in the area.
Scars.prevention: Proper wound care (cleaning and keeping moist) and avoiding picking at scabs.
Scars.locations: Anywhere a skin injury has occurred.
Scars.diagnosis: Based on the history of injury and clinical appearance of the skin.
Scars.immediate_actions: Keep new wounds clean and use a sterile ointment to prevent a thick scab from forming.
Scars.lifestyle: Use high-SPF sunscreen on scars for at least a year after injury to prevent darkening.

Scleroderma.advice: A group of rare diseases that involve the hardening and tightening of the skin and connective tissues.
Scleroderma.cautions: Can be localized (skin only) or systemic (affecting heart, lungs, and kidneys).
Scleroderma.complications: Digital ulcers, pulmonary hypertension, and organ failure in systemic forms.
Scleroderma.solutions: Moisturizers, immunosuppressants, and medications to improve blood flow.
Scleroderma.doctor_advice: Contact a doctor if you experience fingers turning white/blue in the cold and skin thickening.
Scleroderma.symptoms: Hard, thick patches of skin, Raynaud's phenomenon, and joint stiffness.
Scleroderma.prevention: No known prevention; managed through stress reduction and warmth.
Scleroderma.locations: Fingers, hands, face, and occasionally internal organs.
Scleroderma.diagnosis: Skin biopsy, antibody testing (Scl-70, centromere), and capillaroscopy.
Scleroderma.immediate_actions: Keep extremities warm to manage Raynaud's and use heavy emollients.
Scleroderma.lifestyle: Stop smoking, avoid cold temperatures, and monitor for shortness of breath.
visual_features: Loss of hair over affected areas

Seborrheic Dermatitis.advice: A common inflammatory skin condition that causes flaky, white-to-yellowish scales on oily areas.
Seborrheic Dermatitis.cautions: Can be persistent and often flares up in cold weather or during times of stress.
Seborrheic Dermatitis.complications: Secondary fungal or bacterial infection in the affected areas.
Seborrheic Dermatitis.solutions: Anti-dandruff shampoos (ketoconazole, zinc pyrithione) and mild topical steroids for flares.
Seborrheic Dermatitis.doctor_advice: Consult a doctor if the rash is very itchy, becomes red and painful, or doesn't improve with OTC shampoos.
Seborrheic Dermatitis.symptoms: Skin flakes (dandruff), greasy skin covered with flaky scales, and mild redness and itching.
Seborrheic Dermatitis.prevention: Regular use of medicated shampoos and maintaining a healthy scalp hygiene routine.
Seborrheic Dermatitis.diagnosis: Based on the characteristic appearance and location of the rash.
Seborrheic Dermatitis.immediate_actions: Use an over-the-counter anti-dandruff shampoo and avoid heavy hair oils.
Seborrheic Dermatitis.lifestyle: Manage stress and avoid using harsh, alcohol-based skin products.

Seborrheic Keratosis.advice: A benign skin growth common in older adults. It is not cancerous and does not become cancerous.
Seborrheic Keratosis.cautions: Avoid picking at them as they can bleed or become infected. Consult a doctor for confirmation to rule out melanoma.
Seborrheic Keratosis.complications: Irritation, itching, or minor bleeding from clothing friction.
Seborrheic Keratosis.solutions: No treatment needed unless for cosmetic reasons. Options include cryosurgery or curettage.
Seborrheic Keratosis.doctor_advice: Consult a doctor if you see many growths suddenly appear, or if a single growth changes rapidly.
Seborrheic Keratosis.symptoms: Waxy, scaly, slightly raised growths that look 'stuck on' the skin. Usually painless.
Seborrheic Keratosis.prevention: No known prevention as they are largely genetic/age-related.
Seborrheic Keratosis.locations: Face, neck, chest, back, and shoulders.
Seborrheic Keratosis.diagnosis: Visual inspection by a dermatologist; biopsy if it resembles skin cancer.
Seborrheic Keratosis.immediate_actions: Verify with a professional that the lesion is benign.
visual_features: Color ranging from light tan to black

Shingles.advice: Reactivation of the chickenpox virus. Antiviral treatment is most effective when started early.
Shingles.cautions: The rash can be extremely painful. Avoid contact with others, especially pregnant women and newborns.
Shingles.complications: Postherpetic neuralgia (long-term nerve pain) or vision loss if it affects the eye.
Shingles.solutions: Antiviral drugs (acyclovir), pain relievers, and cool compresses.
Shingles.doctor_advice: Seek medical care within 72 hours of the rash starting to reduce the risk of long-term pain.
Shingles.symptoms: Painful rash on one side of the face or body, tingling/burning sensation, and blisters.
Shingles.prevention: Get the shingles vaccine (Shingrix) if you are over 50 or at risk.
Shingles.locations: Often follows a nerve pathway (dermatome) on the torso or face.
Shingles.diagnosis: Based on the appearance and distribution of the rash.
Shingles.immediate_actions: Keep the rash covered and dry. Rest and manage pain with OTC medications.
Shingles.lifestyle: Wear loose cotton clothing and use calamine lotion for itching.
visual_features: Fluid-filled blisters on a red base
Unilateral distribution (only on one side of the body)
Grouped vesicles along a nerve line

Skin Abscess.advice: A painful collection of pus under the skin, usually caused by a bacterial infection (like Staph).
Skin Abscess.cautions: Do not attempt to 'pop' or squeeze the abscess at home, as this can push the infection deeper.
Skin Abscess.complications: Spread of infection (cellulitis), scarring, and potential blood infection (sepsis) if left untreated.
Skin Abscess.solutions: Incision and drainage (I&D) by a professional, and oral antibiotics if necessary.
Skin Abscess.doctor_advice: Seek medical care if the abscess is extremely painful, growing rapidly, or associated with a fever.
Skin Abscess.symptoms: A firm, red, warm, and tender lump. May have a white or yellow 'head' of pus.
Skin Abscess.prevention: Maintain good hygiene, wash hands frequently, and avoid sharing personal items like razors.
Skin Abscess.diagnosis: Clinical examination; culture of the pus to identify the specific bacteria (including MRSA).
Skin Abscess.immediate_actions: Apply warm, moist compresses for 20 minutes several times a day to encourage drainage.
Skin Abscess.lifestyle: Keep the area clean and covered with a sterile bandage if it starts to drain.

Skin Cancer.advice: A generic classification. This could represent BCC, SCC, or Melanoma. Professional evaluation is essential.
Skin Cancer.cautions: Any suspicious skin lesion should be evaluated by a dermatologist. Do not ignore changes.
Skin Cancer.complications: Local invasion, disfigurement, or metastasis depending on the specific cancer type.
Skin Cancer.solutions: Surgical removal (excision, Mohs), radiation, or topical treatments depending on diagnosis.
Skin Cancer.doctor_advice: Schedule an annual full-body skin exam and consult a doctor for any new or changing spots.
Skin Cancer.symptoms: New growths, sores that won't heal, or changes in existing moles.
Skin Cancer.prevention: Sun avoidance, high SPF sunscreen, and protective clothing.
Skin Cancer.locations: Most frequent in sun-exposed areas but possible anywhere on the body.
Skin Cancer.immediate_actions: Consult a dermatologist for a definitive diagnosis.
Skin Cancer.lifestyle: Strict sun protection and regular skin monitoring.

Skin Tags.advice: Small, soft, flesh-colored growths that hang off the skin by a thin stalk (peduncle).
Skin Tags.cautions: Harmless and not contagious; they only need removal if they are irritated or for cosmetic reasons.
Skin Tags.complications: Irritation or bleeding if they get caught on clothing or jewelry.
Skin Tags.solutions: Removal by a doctor using cryotherapy, snip excision, or electrocautery.
Skin Tags.doctor_advice: Consult a doctor if a skin tag becomes painful, bleeds, or changes color (turning black).
Skin Tags.symptoms: Small, skin-colored or brownish growths that are soft to the touch.
Skin Tags.prevention: No known prevention; they are more common in areas of skin-on-skin friction.
Skin Tags.diagnosis: Visual examination by a healthcare provider.
Skin Tags.immediate_actions: Avoid trying to 'tie off' or cut skin tags at home, as this can lead to infection or bleeding.
Skin Tags.lifestyle: Wear smooth fabrics to reduce friction in areas where you are prone to skin tags.
visual_features: Small fleshy papule on a stalk

Spider Angioma.advice: A common vascular lesion characterized by a central red spot with radiating 'legs' of small blood vessels.
Spider Angioma.cautions: Multiple spider angiomas can sometimes be a sign of underlying liver disease or hormone changes.
Spider Angioma.solutions: No treatment needed; laser therapy or electrocautery for cosmetic removal.
Spider Angioma.doctor_advice: Consult a doctor if you suddenly develop many spider angiomas or have other symptoms like jaundice.
Spider Angioma.symptoms: A red spot that pales when pressed and has tiny vessels radiating outward like a spider's legs.
Spider Angioma.prevention: No known prevention; common during pregnancy or with certain medications.
Spider Angioma.locations: Face, neck, upper chest, and arms.
Spider Angioma.diagnosis: Physical examination based on the characteristic 'spider' appearance and blanching.
Spider Angioma.immediate_actions: Monitor for any new lesions or changes in liver health.
Spider Angioma.lifestyle: Protect the skin from the sun to prevent other vascular skin changes.

Squamous Cell Carcinoma.advice: Second most common skin cancer. Can metastasize if not treated promptly.
Squamous Cell Carcinoma.cautions: High risk in immunocompromised patients. Any persistent, scaly, crusty patch should be biopsies.
Squamous Cell Carcinoma.complications: Metastasis to lymph nodes or other organs, local invasion, and recurrence.
Squamous Cell Carcinoma.solutions: Mohs surgery, excision, radiation therapy, or topical treatment for early lesions (SCC in situ).
Squamous Cell Carcinoma.doctor_advice: Seek medical care for any suspicious sore, scaly patch, or raised growth that persists.
Squamous Cell Carcinoma.symptoms: Firm, red nodule, or a flat lesion with a scaly, crusted surface.
Squamous Cell Carcinoma.prevention: Avoid peak sun hours, use high-SPF sunscreen, and wear protective clothing.
Squamous Cell Carcinoma.locations: Face, ears, lips, scalp, hands, and other sun-exposed areas.
Squamous Cell Carcinoma.diagnosis: Visual skin examination followed by punch, shave, or excisional biopsy.
Squamous Cell Carcinoma.immediate_actions: Schedule a dermatology appointment and avoid further sun exposure to the area.
Squamous Cell Carcinoma.lifestyle: Rigorous sun protection and regular dermatologist follow-ups.

Sunburn.advice: Red, painful, and sometimes blistered skin caused by overexposure to ultraviolet (UV) rays from the sun.
Sunburn.cautions: Repeated sunburns significantly increase the lifetime risk of all types of skin cancer.
Sunburn.complications: Pain, dehydration, and second-degree burns with blistering. Premature skin aging.
Sunburn.solutions: Cool baths, aloe vera gel, and moisturizing. Use Ibuprofen for pain and inflammation.
Sunburn.doctor_advice: Consult a doctor for severe blistering, fever, chills, or widespread pain.
Sunburn.symptoms: Red, warm, and tender skin that may peel after a few days.
Sunburn.prevention: Use broad-spectrum SPF 30+ sunscreen, wear protective clothing, and seek shade.
Sunburn.locations: Any area of skin exposed to the sun.
Sunburn.diagnosis: Clinical appearance and history of recent sun exposure.
Sunburn.immediate_actions: Get out of the sun immediately and apply cool compresses to the affected areas.
Sunburn.lifestyle: Make sun protection a daily habit, even on cloudy days.

Telangiectasia.advice: A condition in which small, widened blood vessels cause threadlike red lines or patterns on the skin.
Telangiectasia.cautions: While usually harmless, they can be associated with rosacea, liver disease, or certain genetic disorders.
Telangiectasia.complications: Minor cosmetic concern and occasional mild itching.
Telangiectasia.solutions: Laser therapy or intense pulsed light (IPL) to close the tiny blood vessels.
Telangiectasia.doctor_advice: See a dermatologist for evaluation if the pattern is spreading or associated with facial flushing.
Telangiectasia.symptoms: Thin red or bluish lines that blanch (disappear) when pressed.
Telangiectasia.prevention: Protect skin from the sun and avoid triggers like extreme heat or alcohol if related to rosacea.
Telangiectasia.locations: Face (cheeks and nose), neck, and legs.
Telangiectasia.diagnosis: Visual examination; they have a characteristic appearance and blanching response.
Telangiectasia.immediate_actions: Use sunblock daily to prevent more visible vessels from forming.
Telangiectasia.lifestyle: Avoid harsh skincare products that can irritate sensitive facial skin.
visual_features: Non-palpable red or blue thread-like vessels

Tinea Versicolor.advice: A common fungal infection that causes small, discolored patches. It is not contagious.
Tinea Versicolor.cautions: The patches may become more visible after sun exposure as they do not tan.
Tinea Versicolor.complications: Mainly cosmetic concerns; recurrence is common especially in humid weather.
Tinea Versicolor.solutions: Topical antifungal shampoos (selenium sulfide), lotions, or creams.
Tinea Versicolor.doctor_advice: Consult a doctor if the rash is widespread or does not respond to OTC antifungals.
Tinea Versicolor.symptoms: Painless patches of skin that are lighter or darker than the surrounding area.
Tinea Versicolor.prevention: Avoid excessive heat and sweating; use antifungal washes periodically if prone to it.
Tinea Versicolor.locations: Most common on the chest, back, neck, and upper arms.
Tinea Versicolor.diagnosis: Visual inspection or KOH prep showing 'spaghetti and meatballs' fungus pattern.
Tinea Versicolor.immediate_actions: Apply an OTC antifungal lotion or shampoo to the affected areas.
Tinea Versicolor.lifestyle: Keep skin dry and avoid heavy, oily skincare products.

Ulcers.advice: Open sores on the skin that fail to heal properly, often due to poor circulation or underlying medical conditions.
Ulcers.cautions: Ulcers are prone to deep infection and should never be ignored. They often require specialized wound care.
Ulcers.complications: Cellulitis, bone infection (osteomyelitis), and potential limb loss in severe diabetic cases.
Ulcers.solutions: Wound debridement, compression therapy, specialized dressings, and managing blood sugar/circulation.
Ulcers.doctor_advice: Seek immediate care for any non-healing sore, especially if it is painful, red, or draining pus.
Ulcers.symptoms: An open wound that may be shallow or deep, often with surrounding redness and swelling.
Ulcers.prevention: Manage chronic conditions like diabetes, avoid smoking, and protect skin from trauma.
Ulcers.diagnosis: Physical examination; ultrasound and blood tests to check circulation and glucose levels.
Ulcers.immediate_actions: Keep the wound clean, covered with a sterile bandage, and see a doctor promptly.
Ulcers.lifestyle: Elevate legs to improve circulation and wear comfortable, properly-fitting shoes.
visual_features: Open skin defect with visible basement tissue
Variable bed appearance (pink, yellow, or black)

Urticaria Pigmentosa.advice: The most common form of cutaneous mastocytosis, causing itchy, brown or tan spots on the skin.
Urticaria Pigmentosa.cautions: Rubbing or scratching the spots can cause them to become hive-like (Darier's sign). Avoid triggers like heat.
Urticaria Pigmentosa.complications: Widespread hives and, in rare cases, a severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis).
Urticaria Pigmentosa.solutions: Antihistamines to control itching and avoiding known triggers like certain medications or extreme cold.
Urticaria Pigmentosa.doctor_advice: Consult a dermatologist or allergist for management and to rule out systemic involvement.
Urticaria Pigmentosa.symptoms: Brownish-red spots that itch intensely when rubbed or exposed to warmth.
Urticaria Pigmentosa.prevention: Avoid known triggers like hot baths, vigorous rubbing, and certain pain relievers like aspirin.
Urticaria Pigmentosa.locations: Chest, back, and limbs; less common on the face.
Urticaria Pigmentosa.diagnosis: Clinical examination (Positive Darier's sign); confirmed by skin biopsy showing increased mast cells.
Urticaria Pigmentosa.immediate_actions: Avoid rubbing the spots and see a specialist for a long-term management plan.
Urticaria Pigmentosa.lifestyle: Maintain a list of safe medications to avoid triggering mast cell release.
visual_features: Positive Darier's sign (wheal formation when rubbed)

Vesicles.advice: Small, fluid-filled blisters (less than 1 cm in size) that develop on the surface of the skin.
Vesicles.cautions: Vesicles can be a sign of many things, from simple friction to viral infections like shingles or herpes.
Vesicles.complications: Bacterial infection (impetigo) if the blisters break and are not kept clean.
Vesicles.solutions: Keep the area clean, avoid popping the blisters, and treat the underlying cause.
Vesicles.doctor_advice: Consult a doctor if the blisters are painful, spreading rapidly, or associated with a fever.
Vesicles.symptoms: Small, clear fluid-filled bumps that may be itchy or painful.
Vesicles.prevention: Protect skin from friction and avoid contact with others if a viral cause is suspected.
Vesicles.locations: Anywhere on the skin; often on hands, feet, or face.
Vesicles.diagnosis: Diagnosis is based on the appearance, location, and history of the blisters.
Vesicles.immediate_actions: Do not pop the blisters. Clean with mild soap and cover with a sterile bandage.
Vesicles.lifestyle: Identify triggers like new detergents or exposure to certain plants.

Vitiligo.advice: A condition in which the skin loses its pigment-producing cells (melanocytes), resulting in white patches.
Vitiligo.cautions: White patches are extremely prone to sunburn. Psychological support may be helpful due to social impact.
Vitiligo.complications: Severe sunburn, eye inflammation (uveitis), and association with other autoimmune diseases.
Vitiligo.solutions: Phototherapy (UVB), topical corticosteroids, calcineurin inhibitors, or depigmentation of remaining skin.
Vitiligo.doctor_advice: Consult a dermatologist early as treatments are more effective on newly developed patches.
Vitiligo.symptoms: Loss of skin color in patches, premature whitening of hair on scalp, eyelashes, or eyebrows.
Vitiligo.prevention: No known prevention; focus on protecting affected skin from damage.
Vitiligo.locations: Face, hands, genitalia, and areas around body openings.
Vitiligo.diagnosis: Visual inspection, sometimes using a Wood's lamp (UV light) to highlight depigmented areas.
Vitiligo.immediate_actions: Apply high-SPF (50+) sunscreen to depigmented patches when outdoors.
Vitiligo.lifestyle: Use camouflage makeup if desired; ensure adequate Vitamin D intake as sun exposure is limited.

Warts.advice: Benign skin growths caused by HPV. They often disappear on their own but can take years.
Warts.cautions: They are contagious and can spread through direct contact or shared surfaces.
Warts.complications: Secondary infection, localized pain (plantar warts), or destructive growth around nails.
Warts.solutions: Salicylic acid, cryotherapy (freezing), or laser therapy.
Warts.doctor_advice: See a doctor if warts are painful, bleeding, spreading rapidly, or for cosmetic removal.
Warts.symptoms: Rough, skin-colored, or brown bumps. Can be flat, round, or cauliflower-like.
Warts.prevention: Avoid touching others' warts, wear flip-flops in locker rooms, and keep skin healthy.
Warts.locations: Commonly on hands (common warts), feet (plantar warts), or face (flat warts).
Warts.diagnosis: Visual examination by a healthcare provider.
Warts.immediate_actions: Avoid picking or biting at warts. Keep them covered to prevent spreading.
Warts.lifestyle: Keep hands and feet dry, as HPV thrives in moist environments.
